utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Could the witness be brought in. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Good afternoon, Mrs. Kolesar. If I could remind you of the --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good afternoon.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: -- affirmation you made at the beginning of your evidence which still applies. Mrs. Tuma.

utterances.speaker: MS. TUMA
utterances.text: Thank you. Examined by Ms. Tuma: [Continued]

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Good afternoon, Mrs. Kolesar.

utterances.speaker: BINAZIJA KOLESAR [Resumed]
utterances.text: Good afternoon.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And we will continue where we were yesterday. We ended yesterday's testimony by -- that Mrs. Kolesar mentioned the shelling of the hospital and the city and the surrounding areas. That offered -- created difficult circumstances under which the medical staff and the patients were while they were working or being in the hospital. Can you please tell us if you know of any specific incident that happened when the hospital was targeted by the shelling? Thank you.

utterances.speaker: BINAZIJA KOLESAR [Resumed]
utterances.text: There were several such occasions. What all of us remember, for example, are the airstrikes on the hospital. In one of such attacks a bomb fell on the hospital. It was our estimate that it was 250 kilogrammes. The bomb pierced all of the floors of the new hospital building, all the way down to the underground level, to the basement level, but did not explode. At that point, we were using rainwater. And this is an incident that all of us remember. In addition to that, missiles were fired on the hospital from aeroplanes as well. And when that happened, we went to check the building, and we realised that one part of the hospital building had caved in and was unrecognisable. During that period of time, we got used to those daily attacks on the hospital, but nevertheless, we had to carry on with our work.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you, Mrs. Kolesar. When it comes to the first incident you mentioned here, the 250-kilogramme bomb, did you happen to remember when that was in time?

utterances.speaker: BINAZIJA KOLESAR [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think it was on the 4th or 5th of October. October 1991.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you, Mrs. Kolesar. Were there any efforts made from the hospital side in order to get the shelling to cease, and in what way then?

utterances.speaker: BINAZIJA KOLESAR [Resumed]
utterances.text: Our director, Dr. Bosanac, is -- incessantly sent out appeals and protests or pleas asking that they cease attacking hospital, shelling hospital. We wanted to ensure that the hospital remained operational in order for us to be able to receive the new wounded. For example, we would admit the wounded and put them in a certain portion of the hospital which would be shelled tomorrow, and that was of course very disruptive. So these appeals or pleas were constantly sent out to various persons.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Do you know to whom it was specifically sent to?

utterances.speaker: BINAZIJA KOLESAR [Resumed]
utterances.text: I couldn't really say that I know precisely where they were sent, but it is most likely that every day they were sent out to several places. Dr. Bosanac was in charge of that, and she knew to whom they ought to be sent.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Okay. Thank you, Mrs. Kolesar. And you have told us the great difficulties you did have in the hospital when it comes to taking care of the wounded persons and so on during this time period. Then we are talking about up until mid-November. And were there any kind of evacuation or could the hospital handle with all the wounded persons?

utterances.speaker: BINAZIJA KOLESAR [Resumed]
utterances.text: The hospital had to take in all the wounded persons. There was no alternative. The last large convoy, as I stated yesterday, was on the 19th of October. Sometimes we were able to take several wounded persons at a time to our auxiliary hospital, if I can call it that, which was located in Borovo Naselje. This hospital was also located in the atomic shelter. However, the road to that area was soon thereafter blocked and that became impossible. And from -- from a certain period of time onwards, it was only possible for the wounded persons to be taken to our hospital, and from there we couldn't send them anywhere else.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you, Mrs. Kolesar. When it comes to the 19 October evacuation, who did facilitate that evacuation?

utterances.speaker: BINAZIJA KOLESAR [Resumed]
utterances.text: I suppose it was the JNA, because it was the JNA vehicles that drove away civilians on the 19th. And on the 20th their vehicles drove away our wounded.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now we're talking about October, the 19 October. Were there any other organisations --

utterances.speaker: BINAZIJA KOLESAR [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, yes, the 19th. 19th of October was the day when the convoy was organised by Medicins Sans Frontieres. They managed to arrive. I don't know what kind of negotiations they had with the JNA and how it was made possible for them to get to us, but the fact is that over 100 wounded, or specifically 112 wounded, were evacuated on that occasion, which was a great assistance to us at the time.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Were there any other in the same sense facilitated evacuation done of the 19 October up until the mid-November?

utterances.speaker: BINAZIJA KOLESAR [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I will now return back to the scene, so to say, of the hospital. And were there any -- were the hospital itself defended in any way?

utterances.speaker: BINAZIJA KOLESAR [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know. What do you mean? How can one defend a hospital? I have to put that question, because I really don't know how can a hospital defend itself. There are only medical staff members working in the hospital, so therefore I don't know who would be able to defend the hospital or who would be able to attack it when there are only medical staff there and the wounded.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you, Mrs. Kolesar. Were there any defenders outside the hospital, around the hospital?

utterances.speaker: BINAZIJA KOLESAR [Resumed]
utterances.text: I can't answer that question, because I didn't leave the hospital compound during that period of time, October and November. Therefore, I'm unable to tell you what was going on in the street, whether there were defenders there or not. I really do not know that.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you, Mrs. Kolesar. And how long did the shelling continue on the city of Vukovar? When did the city of Vukovar fell?

utterances.speaker: BINAZIJA KOLESAR [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think that this area where the hospital is located was not shelled any more after the 17th. I don't know whether that date can be taken as the fall of Vukovar. Most likely yes. So that was on the 17th of November.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Okay. Thank you. I will now move on to what happened on specific days.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Mrs. Tuma, could I just interrupt for a moment. I want to clarify something in the transcript that isn't clear to me. We've heard in evidence, Mrs. Kolesar, of two times when wounded were evacuated, one on the 19th of October, and the next time was the 19th and 20th of November. Well, evacuation may not be the word you'd use for the 19th and 20th of November. On the 19th of October, was it the JNA that moved the wounded or was it Medicins Sans Frontieres?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The evacuation was conducted by the organisation called Medicins Sans Frontieres. However, I suppose that they had to agree with the JNA on their route for entering Vukovar. Otherwise, it would have been impossible for them to enter Vukovar. Therefore, it was organised by Medicins Sans Frontieres. And as for their passage, how their passage was arranged, I can only give you my assumptions. I don't know anything more about that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Thank you very much. I'm sorry to have interrupted, Mrs. Tuma.

utterances.speaker: MS. TUMA
utterances.text: That's fine, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I would like to move on, as said, to specific dates, and I will start with the 17th November 1991. Do you remember what happened during that day in the hospital?

utterances.speaker: BINAZIJA KOLESAR [Resumed]
utterances.text: I mostly remember that day by the fact that there was no attack on the hospital. It was very quiet, which was something that we were not used to. The work went on normally in the hospital. There was nothing peculiar going on. There were even no new wounded persons coming in. So it was calm. There was no shooting, and there were no newly wounded persons arriving.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Were there any other persons arriving into the hospital during that day?

utterances.speaker: BINAZIJA KOLESAR [Resumed]
utterances.text: I didn't see them. I didn't see anybody who was not part of the hospital staff.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And how about civilians? Were they arriving to the hospital during that day?

utterances.speaker: BINAZIJA KOLESAR [Resumed]
utterances.text: As soon as it was calm, as soon as there was a lull in the shelling, there would be groups of civilians arriving in the hospital, a large number of civilians coming in from the centre of the town, from all the shelters in the inner urban area. So in the inner urban area there were atomic shelters, and there were also shelters in various private homes, basements, and so on. People believed that the hospital was an oasis of peace where they would be guaranteed salvation, and they were coming to the hospital en masse. It was impossible to prevent them from coming to the hospital. They did not disturb the wounded. They simply occupied various floors of the hospital, or, rather, corridors on all the floors above the basement. In my estimate, there were a thousand people there. Perhaps more, perhaps less, but at any rate there was a huge number of people there. They were children coming in with their sacks, completely beyond themselves, and they were able to find peace there and salvation.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Mrs. Kolesar, you just mentioned there was children with their sacks. Were there any other kind -- can you mention other examples among those 1.000 about or more people that arrived to the hospital during that day, what kind of people it was?

utterances.speaker: BINAZIJA KOLESAR [Resumed]
utterances.text: Those were the people who in the previous three months or, rather, previous 80 days lived in basements. They looked exhausted to me, terrified. I must say that they had to be hungry and thirsty, that they survived on a bare minimum prior to that. They perhaps expected that they would find better conditions in the hospital, but the hospital in fact lived under same conditions as they did. I don't know how to describe a man or a woman or a child to you who spent more than 80 days under abnormal conditions. This is how those people looked.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you, Mrs. Kolesar. Now we will move on to the next day, and that is on the 18th of November. Can you by your own recollection tell us what happened? We can start with the morning. Were there any specific -- or what happened in the morning of the 18th November, if there were anything, so to say?

utterances.speaker: BINAZIJA KOLESAR [Resumed]
utterances.text: Nothing remarkable went on in the hospital except that we were given a task in view of the preparation of the evacuation of the wounded, which was supposed to take place on the 19th of November. We were supposed to compile a list of the wounded. In my view, that list was needed in order to ensure transportation, to arrange transportation, in order to see how many wounded would need transportation in ambulances and how many were able to use some other vehicles and how many were able to sit and so on. So that was our task on the 18th. And it was mostly dealt with by the doctors, because no one else was able to assess what was the most appropriate way to transport a sick person. In addition to that, the staff of the hospital also had to be put on a list. Their names had to be put on a list in order to see what means of transportation were needed. People also had to indicate where they wanted to go. Some wanted to go to Serbia, and some wanted to go to Croatia. Based on that, the lists were compiled.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you, Mrs. Kolesar. I will start with the list you was talking about about the wounded and the sick in the hospital. Who did compile that list? Was it anyone who gave order about that?

utterances.speaker: BINAZIJA KOLESAR [Resumed]
utterances.text: Most likely our director issued an order to the doctors asking them to do that. They had to do it so that she would be able to tell what was needed for evacuation. Without that list, she was unable to say, "I need ten ambulances or ten buses." She had to have some information in order to ask for a certain number of vehicles.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Can you please tell us, Mrs. Kolesar, how that was done, so to say? What measures were taken from the medical staff in order to compile that list? Were there any specific medical staff involved in it? Can you please explain the procedure, how it was done, please.

utterances.speaker: BINAZIJA KOLESAR [Resumed]
utterances.text: For example, I remember that the list was compiled by Dr. Matos, Dr. Tomic. Perhaps somebody else was involved, but I don't know who exactly. It had to be done by several doctors, but right now I can't remember their names. In addition to that, they also had to examine a wounded person and see their medical charts in order to assess what was needed for them. So they couldn't just use the existing documentation. They had to see the actual patient. And this wasn't a job that one could do in half an hour. They actually had to go to see each patient, assess whether he or she was able to sit up or not, and then decide on which list to put that person on the list of the person who could sit up or those who needed ambulances.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Mrs. Kolesar, were you involved in that process in any way to compile the list?

utterances.speaker: BINAZIJA KOLESAR [Resumed]
utterances.text: Only in the technical portion of the job. When the list was compiled, a clerk who worked in the surgical ward and I copied the list or, rather, typed the list on a typewriter, and I helped her in that. So the list that was originally written down by physicians was then retyped on a typewriter. I personally didn't give this list to anybody. This was probably done by our administrative clerk. My job was only to speed up the process.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Do you remember how many names were on this list?

utterances.speaker: BINAZIJA KOLESAR [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. I can't remember, but there were nearly 400 wounded persons. Now, as to who was on which list, I really couldn't tell you that. I don't remember.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: The number 400 wounded, what do you mean by that, Mrs. Kolesar? Can you please explain that?

utterances.speaker: BINAZIJA KOLESAR [Resumed]
utterances.text: Four hundred wounded and ill persons is the category that covered all those who needed medical assistance because they were either -- they had been either wounded or ill. Among those 400 there were newborn babies, women who had just delivered a baby. There were people with various internal disorders, psychiatric patients, and the wounded.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you, Mrs. Kolesar. This list, was that given to a specific person or any person? Do you have any knowledge about that?

utterances.speaker: BINAZIJA KOLESAR [Resumed]
utterances.text: I assume that our clerk, upon a request from the director, gave the list to the director, because the director was the one who initially requested the list. So I suppose that it was turned over to her.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And after that, what was the purpose of the list?

utterances.speaker: BINAZIJA KOLESAR [Resumed]
utterances.text: Most likely in order to know the transportation needs. There was no other purpose for that list. It served no other purpose except to organise an evacuation.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And who was supposed to organise that organisation, that evacuation?

utterances.speaker: BINAZIJA KOLESAR [Resumed]
utterances.text: Once again Dr. Bosanac, in negotiations most likely with the JNA, because who else could she have negotiated with? The city was occupied, occupied by the JNA, so there was nobody else that she could have negotiated with. As for the course of negotiations, I know nothing about that. I had no authorities, nor did I play any role in that regard.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: The International Red Cross, were they in any sense involved in this process?

utterances.speaker: BINAZIJA KOLESAR [Resumed]
utterances.text: We were told that the International Red Cross would be involved in the evacuation, but we didn't see them before the 19th. I still fail to understand what their role would be. With the exception of a lady who came along with a box of medicines to be used in order to help patients during the evacuation, there was no one else. That was on the 19th. This lady gave me the box, and I asked one of our employees to bring the box to the pharmacy.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I'll go back to the 18th. We're still on the 18th, Mrs. Kolesar. In the hospital during that day on the 18th when the lists were compiled, were there presence of any military in the hospital?

utterances.speaker: BINAZIJA KOLESAR [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, personally I have a dilemma. I think some of them got in on the 18th, but probably, since it had been agreed that no one would be going in, it is quite likely that all those that I saw got in on the 19th, into the hospital.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: What do you remember today, Mrs. Kolesar, about -- concerning the 18th? And that day you were talking about a list were compiled about the -- concerning the wounded in the hospital? Do you have any memory on that day that any kind of presence of military in the hospital that you saw yourself?

utterances.speaker: BINAZIJA KOLESAR [Resumed]
utterances.text: There were no soldiers in the hospital. Perhaps there were soldiers around the hospital. We had been advised not to leave the hospital building. Therefore, I was in no position to see whether there were perhaps soldiers outside the hospital building or in the yard. Inside the hospital itself, one certainly couldn't notice any soldiers. On the 18th, we had to prepare the wounded to be evacuated, the evacuation that had been agreed to take place on the 19th. All their wounds had to be dressed. They had to be seen to. They had to be given their personal documents to keep on them when taken elsewhere so that wherever they ended up people would know who they were and what their backgrounds were, what had happened to them. All the documents had to be prepared, and it was down to the patients to keep these documents.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you, Mrs. Kolesar. It's quite a long time ago, of course. It was 1991 this event happened. I will ask you about the son, specific person, about the son of Dr. Ivankovic. Can you tell you anything about him in course of those days?

utterances.speaker: BINAZIJA KOLESAR [Resumed]
utterances.text: Dr. Ivankovic's son came to the hospital. My recollection is slightly blurred, and I might be wrong, but it could have been either on the 18th or the 19th. Both his parents worked at the hospital, and he came to see them. I personally saw him alone -- standing alone talking to his mother. I can't say with certainty whether it was on the 18th or the 19th, but I can say that there were no other soldiers around them at the time when he was visiting his mother.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you, Mrs. Kolesar. In what way was this person dressed when he was visiting the hospital?

utterances.speaker: BINAZIJA KOLESAR [Resumed]
utterances.text: Goran wore a camouflage uniform. He had no cap on, and I didn't see anything else. He was there sitting in this room wearing a camouflage uniform, and he was there in order to talk to his mother.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Mrs. Kolesar, when you mention Goran, is that the first name of the son of Dr. Ivankovic?

utterances.speaker: BINAZIJA KOLESAR [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that's his first name.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you. And, Mrs. Kolesar, when you mention also camouflage uniform, can you by that say what kind of army he then belonged to, by looking at the camouflage uniform?

utterances.speaker: BINAZIJA KOLESAR [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. I'm entirely unfamiliar with that. I did not see any giveaway insignia that might have helped me to identify the uniform.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Is there anything else that you would like to add what happened on the 18 November, Mrs. Kolesar, that you remember?

utterances.speaker: BINAZIJA KOLESAR [Resumed]
utterances.text: The way I remember it, there were no incidents. We were biding our time until the next day when we hoped our wounded would finally be released from this difficult situation and taken away from the hospital that had in the meantime become inadequate to keep them there.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Were you told on that day if the International Red Cross should be involved in any sense in the evacuation that should take place the next day?

utterances.speaker: BINAZIJA KOLESAR [Resumed]
utterances.text: We'd been told that the International Red Cross would be our protection in a way, that the International Red Cross would be there for the evacuation and that they would see to it that the evacuation was well organised and conducted.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: How about the ECMM? Were they in any sense involved?

utterances.speaker: BINAZIJA KOLESAR [Resumed]
utterances.text: Perhaps they were, but none of us, at least those of us inside the hospital, ever laid eyes on them. I don't think there's a single person who could say we saw the European Monitors there, whatever their name was. Then again, they might have been somewhere in the surroundings of the hospital. It's just that we didn't see them.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I would like to move on now to the 19 November and talk specifically about that day. What were -- what was happening on the 19? On the 18 you prepared for evacuation. What was happening on the 19 then?

utterances.speaker: BINAZIJA KOLESAR [Resumed]
utterances.text: The 19th was a massive disappointment because the evacuation had to be postponed. We were hoping to finally get out of that hell. We were hoping that we would be allowed to finally leave and go somewhere, but it turned out not to be possible. For reasons unknown to me, the evacuation was postponed, so we had to go back to treating the wounded, dressing their wounds, making sure they received therapy, feeding them, and giving them water to drink. On the 19th, on the afternoon of the 19th, our janitor Bogdan Kuzmic came into the hospital. He was there to pick up a nurse who had known nothing about her parents' fate for three months, because they had remained in a section of town that had been occupied by the JNA long before. He said he would come back and fetch her one hour later, and he did. On the 19th, the evacuation of civilians also commenced, the civilians who were in the hospital having previously left their shelters. All the civilians who entered the hospital on the 17th were evacuated. Their evacuation was most likely also organised by the JNA, but they had their own lists drawn up by the Red Cross officer for the town of Vukovar, Zeljka Zgonjanin. I'm not sure who had commissioned her to draw up those lists. I can't say anything about that, but she was given a room in our surgical clinic where she compiled those lists and checked them. None of us had anything to do with that, that's her.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Mrs. Kolesar, you said that none of you did anything to do with that. What does that mean? Was it that evacuation of the civilian that entered --

utterances.speaker: BINAZIJA KOLESAR [Resumed]
utterances.text: What I'm trying to say is that we were not involved in the evacuation of civilians. It just wasn't necessary. They could all walk. They got in much the same -- they got out much the same way they got in. Vehicles came for them and they were taken somewhere. I have no idea where. The fact is they left the hospital.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: When was this done during the day of the 19?

utterances.speaker: BINAZIJA KOLESAR [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think, and I can't be certain, it's been a long time, that this began in the afternoon hours and went on. It was November. That's one thing you must take into account. It was dark very soon, and I think the evacuation went on well into the night. That's the way I remember it. At any rate, on the 19th, all of them were taken away from the hospital. Furthermore, on the 19th in the afternoon, Bogdan Kuzmic returned and took that nurse to her parents' place. I was told that he had again returned to the hospital and took away three other persons belonging to our medical staff. That's at least what people told me later on. This is not something that I personally witnessed at the time.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Mrs. Kolesar, you mentioned about -- that it was a massive disappointment that there was no evacuation done on the 19th November of the wounded and sick. Were you or your staff informed about the reason for that?

utterances.speaker: BINAZIJA KOLESAR [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. No. All we now was the evacuation was postponed, and we were told that it would probably take place on the 20th, but no explanations were provided. We could only speculate that no vehicles were available, something like that, but these were mere assumptions. We didn't know what the reasons behind it were. We knew that it was postponed and that we had to wait for the next day.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And did you have any knowledge about on the 19 who should facilitate, who should perform the evacuation of the wounded and sick out of the hospital?

utterances.speaker: BINAZIJA KOLESAR [Resumed]
utterances.text: We knew that the JNA would be organising that and that the International Red Cross would be monitoring and checking the whole process. That's what we had been told the day before. We expect it had would happen on the 19th, but then this is what we were told.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Also on the 19, you said here that the massive -- the massive number of civilians were evacuated after -- out of the hospital until the dark hours. By that means did you see any military? Was there any kind of military presence inside the hospital at the time during that day on the 19 November?

utterances.speaker: BINAZIJA KOLESAR [Resumed]
utterances.text: With the exception of certain individuals coming in, going out, like Kuzmic, I did not see anyone else. I did not meet anyone else.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you, Mrs. Kolesar. I would like to move on to the next day, and that is the 20th of November. And before going into specific questions, I would like you, Mrs. Kolesar, to once again look on your made chart on your right-hand side, and I would like the Court and the parties to look at number, and the court officer here, that is the ERN number that we had yesterday. It's 04639058. Okay. Just a moment, Mrs. Kolesar. What is going to be prepared.

utterances.speaker: BINAZIJA KOLESAR [Resumed]
utterances.text: Very well.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: In the night, during the night, Mrs. Kolesar -- just a moment, please. During the night between the 19th and 20th November, where were you sleeping then?

utterances.speaker: BINAZIJA KOLESAR [Resumed]
utterances.text: I wouldn't exactly use the word sleeping. I was trying to get some rest. That's what I was doing. I used the room that we refer to as unclean in the hospital. It was in the internal ward. It was the -- our own lingo that we used. We called it the unclean room. The window panes had been shattered, and it was cold, but at least we could lie down on some crates that were in the room. My husband and I spend the night there. We tried to rest there. Before I left this room I was supposed to report my whereabouts, just in case any new wounded came in. I had to speak to the duty anaesthesiologist so that he would know where I was in case new wounded came in. We had to know where to put them. I spent the night in this unclean room on the ground floor.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And in the morning, Mrs. Kolesar, what happened? We take step by step. What happened in the morning on the 20th November?

utterances.speaker: BINAZIJA KOLESAR [Resumed]
utterances.text: The next morning, it's difficult to say what time it was exactly but it was still dark, it might have been around 7.00 a.m., Dr. Kust came to fetch me, telling me that I had to go down to the surgical clinic. I followed him there. The door of the plaster room inside the surgical clinic --

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Could you show on the chart here where that room was located?

utterances.speaker: BINAZIJA KOLESAR [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. It's right here.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Can you please --

utterances.speaker: BINAZIJA KOLESAR [Resumed]
utterances.text: There's a dot here.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Can you also please mark it with a number, please, Mrs. Kolesar. You can say number 1.

utterances.speaker: BINAZIJA KOLESAR [Resumed]
utterances.text: All right. [Marks].

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: It occurs to me, Mrs. Tuma, that there have been very many positions marked and none of them numbered, and it may be now is a good time to number what is there.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Fine.

utterances.speaker: MS. TUMA
utterances.text: Yes, we can do that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Mrs. Kolesar, you have marked with a number 1 the entrance which you've just done. I wonder whether you could mark with a number 2 the -- and put a circle around it, the new building, the main new building of the hospital.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] It's marked.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Put a circle around the number 2, please.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] [Marks].

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: And if you could mark with a number 3 the old building and put a circle around 3, please.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] [Marks].

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Could you mark with a number 4 the atomic shelter and put a circle around that.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] [Marks].

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: With a number 5, the underground corridor.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] [Marks].

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Thank you. With a number 6, the hospital yard.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] [Marks].

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: With a number 7, the main entrance to the hospital.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] [Marks].

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Thank you. With a number 8, the second entrance that you mentioned, the one at Cesta Road.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] [Marks].

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: With a number 9, the surgical clinic.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] [Marks].

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: And with a number 10, two number 10s, each one being where the canvas Red Cross signs were.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] [Marks].

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Sorry, number 10.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Just a minute, please. I'm placing the number 6 here, and there's the yard behind the building. There's one between the two buildings, and there's a lawn behind one of the buildings. I've marked both with the number 6.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Both those yards are lawns.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues]....

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] And I'm using number 10 to mark this.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Thank you. As I recall it, Mrs. Tuma, they are the main features that were described and marked yesterday by the witness.

utterances.speaker: MS. TUMA
utterances.text: That is correct, Your Honour. Thank you so much for this.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: And I thought it could be useful to get those identified at this point.

utterances.speaker: MS. TUMA
utterances.text: Excellent, Your Honour. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: So you're asking now about the entrance to the surgical clinic, and you carry on from there.

utterances.speaker: MS. TUMA
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Yes, Mrs. Kolesar. You just marked the room. Was it so? Yes. And what happened now? We go back so we can start over again. What happened now in the morning on the 20th November?

utterances.speaker: BINAZIJA KOLESAR [Resumed]
utterances.text: I entered this room with Dr. Kust, the so-called plaster room. During the war it was used as an operations room. I found Dr. Ivankovic right there. Also, there were two persons wearing JNA uniform inside, one of them a camouflage uniform and the other being something that struck me as the regulation JNA uniform. Dr. Ivankovic said that the person wearing the standard regulation JNA uniform was a doctor who wished to inspect a number of the wounded. He had a list with their names, so off we went. The first name on the list was the husband of one of our nurses. Of course there was no way for me to know which bed he was in, or maybe Dr. Ivankovic assumed that I would be able to track them down immediately. I had to ask around. I had to consult nurses working in different rooms around the hospital where this person was, and they pointed me in the right direction. So we passed the surgery corridor, the polyclinic. We passed through the underground corridor and reached the old hospital. The person they were looking for was in one of the rooms in that building, and then he was called so that -- I'm listening.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Sorry to interrupt you, Mrs. Kolesar. Before I forget the question.

utterances.speaker: BINAZIJA KOLESAR [Resumed]
utterances.text: The lady doctor came out with him, the one who was in charge of this patient. She told the doctor that his eye had been injured. They took the bandage off so that he could inspect it himself, and then we just continued our round. We did manage to find some of the people from his list, and he examined them. There were some people we weren't able to find, but he wasn't really adamant that he should tick off all the names on the list. After this inspection or whatever you might choose to call it, we returned to this room that we referred to as the plaster room.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Okay. Thank you, Mrs. Kolesar. We'll stop there and I would like to go back with some questions about this, this phase, so to say, on the morning of the 20th of November. You say there was one of the people in the room you were just explaining that were hand -- that did have the list. Was it so?

utterances.speaker: BINAZIJA KOLESAR [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, the doctor.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And what kind of list was that?

utterances.speaker: BINAZIJA KOLESAR [Resumed]
utterances.text: This was not the list containing the names of the wounded that we had compiled. This was just a small list or a short memo, something that could have been based on one of our own lists. But I don't know in what way. I have no idea who produced this short list that the doctor had. The fact is, he asked to see a number of our wounded. Based on what or what the criteria were for the names selected, I have no idea. Perhaps to determine how they would be taken away or perhaps to look at their case histories. I have no idea what he had in mind, what the purpose was of this inspection, but he certainly wasn't very persistent. He wasn't adamant that all the names and all the people should be checked. He just rushed straight through it. We did a pretty quick job, and we were being escorted throughout by an armed soldier. Soon after, we were back to the plaster room. We covered the entire area and all the rooms where the wounded were, virtually all of it.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Mrs. Kolesar, when you said that -- I'm going back now to what happened in the morning and the examination of the patient. How many about were there time to examine? How many did the -- the doctor examine from that specific list, how many wounded?

utterances.speaker: BINAZIJA KOLESAR [Resumed]
utterances.text: Very brief, perhaps 15 to 20 minutes. It's hard to say. The time that we needed to get to the end of the underground corridor, to locate the wounded on the list, to take the bandages off, examined their wounds, and that was it. The list wasn't short, so the whole endeavour didn't take long.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did you see any member from the ICRC or the European Monitors at the hospital in the morning when this event took -- did happen?

utterances.speaker: BINAZIJA KOLESAR [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, no one.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did you see Dr. Vesna Bosanac, Mrs. Bosanac at the time? This is in the morning?

utterances.speaker: BINAZIJA KOLESAR [Resumed]
utterances.text: At that time when this examination went on, I didn't see her then. Following this, upon my return to the plaster room, an order had already been issued to assemble all medical staff from all rooms in the plaster room. All males and all the wounded who were able to walk had to leave the premises and walk towards the courtyard. So by the time we got back another order had been issued, and medical staff started streaming into the plaster room slowly. I say slowly because some of them were on the floors sleeping there. Some of them were in distant premises. So it took time for all of them to assemble in the plaster room. In addition to that, the wounded persons who were able to walk, male persons who were in the hospital for whatever reason, started leaving the hospital building.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Okay, Mrs. Kolesar. We can stop there.

utterances.speaker: BINAZIJA KOLESAR [Resumed]
utterances.text: Just a second, please. In the meantime, a doctor who wanted to go to Belgrade claimed that he didn't know that there was a list of staff members who wanted to go to this place or that place. I knew the office that Dr. Bosanac used, and I went there. I saw Dr. Bosanac sitting there. With her there was our government commissioner, Marin Bilic, Bili, and there was another uniformed and armed person there. I approached the -- I approached Dr. Bosanac asking for the list, and she told me where it was, and I took it. That was the first and last day -- last time on that day that I saw Dr. Bosanac. I don't know what happened to her afterwards. She didn't come out of the building with us and didn't go into the courtyard. That was the last time I saw her.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you, Mrs. Kolesar. I would like now to go back in what happened. You said that you returned back to this plaster room, was that correct, after the examination of the patients?

utterances.speaker: BINAZIJA KOLESAR [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's right.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And who were in that room at that time when you returned back?

utterances.speaker: BINAZIJA KOLESAR [Resumed]
utterances.text: In that room there was a man wearing a camouflage uniform and the doctor who examined the patients with me and some of our doctors. Our doctors, some of them knew this person. Later on I learned from Dr. Njavro that his name as Ivezic. So some of our doctors knew him perhaps from medical school or elsewhere. People started coming in and all of us assembled there. We were all waiting to hear the news, to hear when the evacuation would start and so on. So I suppose once all of us in assembled, all medical staff, male and female, Dr. Ivezic addressed us, telling us said Dr. Bosanac was no longer director and that he was now the person in command of the hospital. Following that, another person addressed us. I'm not sure about his rank. I suppose it was major. At any rate, Mr. Sljivancanin addressed us and gave a speech. Let's call it a speech. I don't know whether you're interested in the content of this speech. I don't think it's anything interesting.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Mrs. Kolesar, I would like to interrupt you here now. Now we are talking about -- you're talking about what happened in the plaster room. First you went out, examined with the wounded together with a doctor from the list, and then you returned back to the plaster room. And who were there? There were medical staff in that plaster room? Were there also Sljivancanin present in that room at that time?

utterances.speaker: BINAZIJA KOLESAR [Resumed]
utterances.text: Most likely, yes, because I didn't see any other soldiers coming in except for the one wearing a camouflage uniform who introduced himself as Veselin Sljivancanin and told us that the evacuation of the wounded had already started, that we would wait for the buses, and nothing else. So it was a speech which took -- I couldn't say how much time.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did Sljivancanin gave any orders or instructions in that room?

utterances.speaker: BINAZIJA KOLESAR [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. We did not receive any specific instructions except that we were to wait for -- or, rather, while all of us were in the plaster room, the males had left the hospital. We were told that we could get our belongings and go to the yard to wait for the buses there.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: All you said here, Mrs. Kolesar, that the wounded should leave as well the hospital. When was that said and by whom?

utterances.speaker: BINAZIJA KOLESAR [Resumed]
utterances.text: If you are referring to the wounded who were able to walk, I don't know who issued that order. All I know is that we were told that all those wounded who were able to walk and all males should go out into the yard. The wounded who were unable to move remained in their beds expecting evacuation, awaiting evacuation.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So all the wounded that could walk and all men should go out of the hospital; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: BINAZIJA KOLESAR [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's right. Not only they were supposed to go out, but they actually did go out. All men simply walked out. It wasn't up to them to decide. We had a male nurse who knew the premises really well. We were supposed to tell them, to give them a person, to assign a person to them who knew the hospital really well, and that person toured the hospital with them to ensure that no one stayed back. So the hospital had been inspected.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did you see that, Mrs. Kolesar, that all men and all the wounded that could walk went out of the hospital?

utterances.speaker: BINAZIJA KOLESAR [Resumed]
utterances.text: I can't say that I saw all the men going out, but as we were preparing to go into the plaster room some men passed by us. They were going out through the emergency room entrance. They went out through that entrance into the yard, and I don't know where they were taken from there.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Can you please show us on the chart here, Mrs. Kolesar, what you were just said about some of the men and the wounded?

utterances.speaker: BINAZIJA KOLESAR [Resumed]
utterances.text: All right. So the basement of the old building, underground corridor, atomic shelter, all of the areas of the new building which were used as patient rooms, all of these were areas from which the wounded who were able to walk came out as well as men. They all came out to the emergency room entrance. There was another door that they could have used through the gynaecological clinic. I don't know if they use that had door or not, but most of them went out through the surgical clinic entrance. While we were assembling there, we were able to see a group of people standing one behind the other facing the road marked with number 8.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And this group of people, Mrs. Kolesar, what was it compiled of?

utterances.speaker: BINAZIJA KOLESAR [Resumed]
utterances.text: This group comprised, let's say our employees, our husbands who were in the hospital, people from the working group, and so on.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: What gender was it on those people that were standing in that group?

utterances.speaker: BINAZIJA KOLESAR [Resumed]
utterances.text: Men.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you, Mrs. Kolesar. What happened next?

utterances.speaker: BINAZIJA KOLESAR [Resumed]
utterances.text: Following that, we were told that we could get ready to leave. As I have told you, there were staff members of both sex among our group. We started getting ready to leave the hospital. And as I was getting ready, I saw in front of the surgical clinic the remaining portion of the medical staff, which comprised only women and their children. They stood there awaiting evacuation.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Mrs. Kolesar, where were the men then? Did you see them at that specific time when you saw the children and the women?

utterances.speaker: BINAZIJA KOLESAR [Resumed]
utterances.text: At one point those men were no longer there, but I have to go to a period of time prior to that when one of our nurses saw her husband leaving the hospital and that he also was in the line with others. While we were in the plaster room, Mr. -- and when Mr. Sljivancanin told us that we could leave, she asked where our husbands were. Then Mr. Sljivancanin said that we should compile a list, and another nurse did that, and she put a list in his hands. We were then able to leave the plaster room. We didn't know where our husbands were. We didn't know why we compiled the list, but list was, nevertheless, compiled and given to Mr. Sljivancanin. Once we picked our belongings, then we saw the other female staff members. All of us walked towards the yard marked with number 6, which was in front of the emergency room. There were very many of us there. I couldn't give you the number. We were told to wait for the buses which would take us to our destinations.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Okay, Mrs. Kolesar. We can stop there for a while. You said that there was a nurse. Do you remember her -- her name, by any chance? Whose husband were in the line.

utterances.speaker: BINAZIJA KOLESAR [Resumed]
utterances.text: The nurse who noticed that the men were going somewhere was called Mara Bucko. She was a long-time staff member, and her husband, along with many other husbands, was also at the hospital.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: What did she do?

utterances.speaker: BINAZIJA KOLESAR [Resumed]
utterances.text: What do you mean?

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did she approach any person about her husband?

utterances.speaker: BINAZIJA KOLESAR [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, no. We stood together in a group and she simply approached Mr. Sljivancanin, asking him where our husbands were. So she didn't, in fact, go to stand close to him but, rather, addressed him while standing among us. And then she told that he should write up a list and that was done very quickly, and the list was turned over to Mr. Sljivancanin. Then we went into the yard together with all other staff members. We waited for the buses. Naturally, we had no idea at the time where our husbands were and where were the wounded who were able to walk. There was no way for us to know what was actually happening. We all believed that the evacuation had just started. We had no idea where they were and how come they were not with us.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: That -- I'm referring back to the list that Mr. Sljivancanin asked that should be put together. Who were there on that list? What kind of categories of people were put on that list?

utterances.speaker: BINAZIJA KOLESAR [Resumed]
utterances.text: Mostly our husbands. So the husbands of medical staff. And only medical staff spouses, those who were in the plaster room. The other staff members who were not assembled in the plaster room did not have an occasion to put this question. So at the time, we did not know what was going on. We didn't know -- not know why we were asked to draw up this list, and we didn't know what was going on with our husbands.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Mrs. Kolesar, can you -- have you any knowledge about how many names were on that list with the husbands of the medical staff?

utterances.speaker: BINAZIJA KOLESAR [Resumed]
utterances.text: I didn't see the list because another person wrote down the names. I can't tell you the exact number of names that was on the list, but I can tell you the names of the persons who later on returned and whose names were on the list. But I can't tell you whether all of those people returned because I don't know that. Some of the persons returned later, but I couldn't tell you whether all of the persons from the list returned.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Okay. During this process, did you see any presence of the ICRC or ECMM at the hospital?

utterances.speaker: BINAZIJA KOLESAR [Resumed]
utterances.text: As we were waiting in the compound for the buses, we didn't see anyone. We were only able to see that the JNA ambulances entered the compound. We assumed that the evacuation of the wounded who needed to be transported in ambulances had started. There were many JNA ambulances which passed us.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And did you see any representative from the ICRC or ECMM during this time, this process at the hospital?

utterances.speaker: BINAZIJA KOLESAR [Resumed]
utterances.text: In the hospital compound where we were, none of them were present, either next to the surgical ward entrance or in any other part of the compound where we were. No member of either organisation was there, at least as far as we could see.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Were you awaiting them to be present there?

utterances.speaker: BINAZIJA KOLESAR [Resumed]
utterances.text: Naturally we did, especially once some of the wounded had left without us seeing anyone. Therefore, we didn't know what was going on. We didn't know whether they were standing somewhere outside of the compound. We didn't know why some of the wounded had left, why and where to. That was just something we didn't know.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Mrs. Kolesar, you just mentioned the JNA ambulances. Can you tell us more about that? How many ambulances did arrive? Did you see it? And what did they do at the hospital?

utterances.speaker: BINAZIJA KOLESAR [Resumed]
utterances.text: We saw the ambulances pass by. I personally didn't count them. But since the ambulances came to the emergency room entrance, we who were standing in the yard were physically unable to see the evacuation of the wounded. The doctors remained in the compound, those who were supposed to accompany the wounded, and the nurses who were on duty at the time. Those who were seriously wounded needed medical attendance en route while they were transported. Therefore, some of the doctors remained there to do that, whereas others who were not on duty stood with us in the compound awaiting the buses.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Okay. Thanks a lot.

utterances.speaker: BINAZIJA KOLESAR [Resumed]
utterances.text: I would like to ask for something.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Yes, please?

utterances.speaker: BINAZIJA KOLESAR [Resumed]
utterances.text: It was probably my mistake that we skipped over one portion. Some of the wounded who were examined by Dr. Marko Ivezic, who were unable to walk, there were perhaps four to six of them, were taken out prior to anybody else. This was done by the nurses who worked on orders of Dr. Ivankovic. Where these people were taken, in what vehicles, I don't know because I didn't see that. All I know is that they were taken from the place where they were. So this pertains to the wounded examined by Dr. Ivezic. I apologise that I omitted to say this earlier when I was describing the events.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: That's fine, Mrs. Kolesar. When it comes to who was -- in what way were -- was Mr. Sljivancanin active in the hospital when you were in any way in contact with him? Now we're talking about the time frame that you were together with the other standing outside on the yard, what you did see yourself.

utterances.speaker: BINAZIJA KOLESAR [Resumed]
utterances.text: Later on in the yard, I never saw Mr. Sljivancanin. I only saw him in the surgical clinic. We listened to what he had to say. He department listen to us. We listened to him. So we saw him as a person addressing us, telling us something, the person of importance, probably. There was no reason for us to talk to him or approach him, at least not individually.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You said right now that he was a person of some importance. By what means then? Can you expand on that a little bit, Mrs. Kolesar?

utterances.speaker: BINAZIJA KOLESAR [Resumed]
utterances.text: It was my impression that with everything that was going on there he was actually the person issuing orders and telling people what to do. He was the one who said, "Draw up a list," and he was the one who said, "You can go. You can get ready to leave," and so on. I can't tell you anything beyond that. At the time, at the moment where our husbands were is brought in from somewhere else, I also approached Mr. Sljivancanin asking for help, but we will get to that once we start talking about the moment when our husbands were brought in and taken off the buses.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you, Mrs. Kolesar.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: That, Mrs. Tuma, may be a convenient time, I think.

utterances.speaker: MS. TUMA
utterances.text: Excellent, Your Honour. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: We will resume at five minutes past 4.00.

utterances.speaker: MS. TUMA
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Yes, Mrs. Tuma.

utterances.speaker: MS. TUMA
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Okay. Mrs. Kolesar, we left when -- before the break here when men and women were separated and you were out standing on the yard. And how did you find out where your husband was at the time?

utterances.speaker: BINAZIJA KOLESAR [Resumed]
utterances.text: As we were standing outside the hospital, one of the husbands approached us. His nose was bleeding and his mouth was bleeding too. He was all covered in blood. He walked in our direction and told us, "Your husbands are over there." We asked, "What do you mean by over there?" And he said they were on a bus near the place that I marked as number 8. We were now allowed to go and get them. When I say "we," I mean the persons who wrote down the names of their husbands on Mr. Sljivancanin's list, the list that was handed over to him. I was one of the people who went. I saw my husband on that bus. He was no longer wearing the same clothes as when he had left. He was wearing a track suit, but he no longer had the winter coat on. He looked slightly lost. I got onto the bus. The bus was guarded by a soldier carrying a rifle. He asked me what I was looking for. I said, "There's my husband there." And he said I couldn't go and talk to him or take him away. Some of the women were allowed to take their husbands away. On my way back, I asked Dr. Ivankovic and Dr. Stanojevic to help me. They said there was nothing they could do. I spoke to Mr. Sljivancanin. He said, "If he's on the bus, they will let him go." So I went back but to no avail. The nurse we mentioned a while ago, Mara Bucko, and I talked to Mr. Ivezic [realtime transcript read in error "Ivankovic"] asking him to try and help us. He said he needed people to help him, to work for him, asked if we were willing to go back and give him a hand. He -- we said that we -- that he should first let us go and then we would eventually come back. He came with us and he helped to get our husbands released from the bus. They looked a bit strange. At first it was impossible to find out where they had been or what had happened. My husband, for example, was limping. He said that he had been hit on his knee. They had to run a gauntlet, as it were, made up of paramilitaries who beat them. They were then put on a bus and told that they would be executed. But eventually they brought them outside the hospital probably the execution bit was just an attempt to intimidate them. Our husbands who got off the buses - of course this is something we only found out later on - were the only men who had been taken away and survived.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Excuse me.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Lukic.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I think that there is an error in the transcript on page 34, 33, rather, line 17. I think the witness mentioned Dr. Ivezic. What the transcript reflects is Dr. Ivankovic. Maybe this needs clarifying. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Lukic.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Dr. Ivankovic. You can mention both of them, as a matter of fact. I spoke to both of them. I spoke to Dr. Ivankovic, which may not have been included in the transcript, or Dr. Stanojevic for that matter. But Dr. Ivezic is the one who helped us to get our husbands off that bus.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you, Mrs. Kolesar. You mentioned earlier here about this incident, that you were allowed to go. You started your answer by saying that. Who did allow you to go away in order to find out where your husbands were?

utterances.speaker: BINAZIJA KOLESAR [Resumed]
utterances.text: No one, really. We weren't being watched by guards. We were standing in the courtyard. We were free. I'm not sure if I would have been allowed to leave and go back to town, for example, not that I tried, but no one stood in my way although I didn't even try to leave the hospital compound as it were. All this time I remained in the area between the hospital and the road where the bus was, but no one stood in my way.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you, Mrs. Kolesar. You also said the bus were guarded by a soldier with a rifle. Can you tell us what kind of soldier that was, if you know that by your own knowledge? Describe him, uniform.

utterances.speaker: BINAZIJA KOLESAR [Resumed]
utterances.text: My impression is it was a uniformed soldier. I think it was a camouflage uniform, but I can't be certain. He was carrying some sort of rifle which I couldn't describe. But I'm certain that he was carrying a weapon.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Was there more than one soldier? You said a soldier. You said it was just one soldier?

utterances.speaker: BINAZIJA KOLESAR [Resumed]
utterances.text: On the bus, you mean?

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: BINAZIJA KOLESAR [Resumed]
utterances.text: I only saw one guard. As for the area around the bus, I can't say that I saw anyone else. But it's difficult to remember now whether I noticed anyone else wearing a uniform. I must say I wasn't exactly looking around. I had one aim in mind: The bus and my husband. I wasn't in the mood to look around much and see who else was there. I can't say whether there were any military or paramilitary persons there. I had my mind set on getting to that bus and getting to my husband, and it's all I can really talk about.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you, Mrs. Kolesar. And you said also that you spoke to Mr. Sljivancanin. Can you tell us more about that? Why did you seek him out, or why did you spoke to him?

utterances.speaker: BINAZIJA KOLESAR [Resumed]
utterances.text: I believed that he was someone who could help me, that he was the person to speak to because he was the one that we'd given the list with our husbands' names to. As they were already on the bus, he looked like someone who might be able to tell them to release those people. It seemed like perfectly reasonable thing to do, for me to go and speak to him. He did not refuse to help me, but he did not help me either. He just said if he's on the bus, he will get out. That is what he said, and that is what eventually happened.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you, Mrs. Kolesar. Now we'll move on to your husband. You saw that he was injured, that he had blood on himself and that a nose and a mouth was injured. What did he tell you what has happened to him?

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Objection, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] My husband was not injured.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: I think your objections being dealt with, Mr. Lukic.

utterances.speaker: MS. TUMA
utterances.text: Thank you. Thank you for that.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, precisely. The first person to leave the bus was the person who was bleeding. I didn't really notice that any of the other persons there were bleeding, that their noses were bleeding, but my husband was limping. His right knee had been hit. He probably saw what was going on, wherever they had been. He had used his arms to protect his head but he was hit -- or, rather, kicked in the stomach and in the knee. He suffered the consequences of this blow until the day he died. He always complained about this injured knee. It kept giving him a lot of trouble. I can't say how the others fared, I can only talk about what I saw. But they certainly told other people about how they'd been kicked and hit.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did your husband tell you who did or whom did hit him and in what way and where?

utterances.speaker: BINAZIJA KOLESAR [Resumed]
utterances.text: According to their accounts, our husbands were first taken to the barracks. Their names were called out according to the lists that we had provided. They got off the bus one by one, and they needed to get to the other bus that was to drive them back. A gauntlet was formed there, as the expression that springs to mind, made up of -- I'm not sure whether those people were paramilitary soldiers, regular military personnel, or whoever, and he didn't know either. They had to run this gauntlet, in a manner of speaking. And as they were running, they were all kicked and beaten. Some more and some less, but all of them were hit at some point. Why were they beaten and kicked I have no idea, and probably he didn't have one either.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you, Mrs. Kolesar. Were there other husbands on the -- that bus when we're talking about? Were they also released at this specific time, as your own husband?

utterances.speaker: BINAZIJA KOLESAR [Resumed]
utterances.text: Most were. I did hear, though, that there were two persons who never left that bus. Two persons, and these are their last names, Zeljko and Adzaga, the former a cook and the latter someone's husband or someone who worked in the hospital compound. I'm not sure. Those two never left the bus, and nobody knew what had become of them at the time. However, later their bodies were identified at Ovcara. Also, based on what I heard, one of our male nurses was taken away on that bus. Eventually he ended up in the camp at Mitrovica. That's about all I know about who was on that bus and who got away. I'm not sure about their exact number, and I'm not even sure whether all of those who were actually on the list were on the bus as I've said already.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you, Mrs. Kolesar. What happened later on after this point of time with you and your husband?

utterances.speaker: BINAZIJA KOLESAR [Resumed]
utterances.text: My husband and I were standing in the place as all the other hospital employees within the hospital compound. At the time the buses arrived, we left the main hospital entrance, number 7, down the path some distance from the hospital where we remained and were told to wait for the buses. We spent quite a lot of time waiting in the buses eventually arrived. We were then loaded onto these buses, and at some time, it may have been half past 1.00 or 2.00, we left and drove to the centre of town. We passed through the centre of town and turned off towards a neighbourhood known as Sajmiste. The bus pulled over outside the Velepromet warehouse. I didn't know the reason why we stopped there. We remained there for some time. No one left the bus and no one got onto the bus, at least on my bus. After a while, we continued our journey. First we took a right turn, the road lead to go Bogdanovci, then we made a semicircle, because we were told at one point that we can proceed down that road, so we drove back to the same road as previously and made another turn towards Negoslavci. We stopped at Negoslavci. I assume the reason was to let through the military vehicles en route from Negoslavci for the centre of town. And the other reason was we were told to wait for the convoy carrying the wounded to catch up. So we stayed there for some time, and eventually the military medical vehicles were there. A column of vehicles was formed. There was a vehicle with some sort of a rotating light driving in front of us. It wasn't night really, but it was late afternoon and it was already quite dark. We got to the village of Negoslavci. One thing I can't fail to mention is Negoslavci, unlike what we saw on our way through Vukovar, was a village that was still intact, no houses having been destroyed. It had the public lighting in perfectly good working order, and everybody appeared to be leading a perfectly normal existence, unlike what we had witnessed in Vukovar itself, which was a town full of ruins. Occasionally we would also spot dead bodies by the roadside. And the town itself had been destroyed beyond recognition. The area around Velepromet, which is more or less the same area as the barracks, was perfectly intact. Maybe there was a house missing a roof tile or something like that, but for the most part it was perfectly intact. We then left Negoslavci. I was thinking that maybe once we reached the main road we would turn off and drive towards Croatia, but we took the turn leading to Serbia, and we drove all the way to Sremska Mitrovica. We stopped in Sremska Mitrovica. Again, I can't say why. People were already exhausted because we'd been driving a long time. Some people were thirsty. Some needed a cigarette. Some needed to use the toilet. People would go into private houses nearby where the bus stopped, but then we continued our journey and eventually reached the sports hall, the gym, and that was where we first noticed people in white, those who were supposed to be in Vukovar, who were supposed to be escorting us. But that was where we first came across them. They told us not to leave the buses. They told us to compile lists with exact numbers of people on the buses and so on and so forth, despite which several people got off the buses and went into the hall. One of our young doctors found her mother, daughter and two children there. One of our nurses found her husband there. And they all returned to our bus. As we'd been told not to leave our buses, we were driven from this gym or sports hall to the compound of the medical hospital. We were offered tea. In the medical station building, we found out that our wounded were already there who had been brought in by ambulance. They were just lying around in rooms and in corridors inside that building. The staff that was with them throughout was still with them. We went back to our buses. We were being watched by guards. And we spent the night on the buses. We realised that not all of our wounded had been brought in, had been brought to Sremska Mitrovica from the hospital on that afternoon and that more vehicles would be going back to Vukovar in the course of the afternoon to fetch the remaining -- the remaining wounded. There were still about 70 of those in the hospital, and at the health station there were already about 120 of those. And indeed after some time, the remaining wounded were eventually brought in. There was a column of ambulances and buses that formed, and we left Mitrovica and drove off in the direction of Bosnia. We were surprised to see that the buses with men and those wounded who were still able to walk were missing. We knew nothing about what happened become of those buses, nor was anyone able to tell us about that. On our way to Bosnia, there was some sort of a spa there. We stopped there and noticed that medical vehicles from Croatia started arriving as well as buses with Croatian registration plates.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Mrs. Kolesar, I would like to interrupt you there. I'm sorry. What were your final -- which were your final direction? Where did you end up and on what date?

utterances.speaker: BINAZIJA KOLESAR [Resumed]
utterances.text: Most of those who were in the hospital opted to go back to Croatia. We didn't know where we were being taken nor did we really have a say in it, but our destination was Croatia. Some of the staff working with us at the hospital opted to go to Serbia and were given a special bus to go there. We were perfectly happy that at some point we finally crossed the bridge over the Sava. We reached Slavonski Samac, and we knew that we were now on Croatian territory. Most of us reached our destinations the next morning. What I wanted was to go to Zagreb since my two daughters lived there. It was on the 22nd, in the morning hours, that my husband and I eventually reached Zagreb. In the meantime, however, on the 21st, in Mitrovica, my mother had died. I didn't stay there to attend her funeral, but the military personnel from the military medical station took over the task of organising the funeral, and she was eventually buried at the Mitrovica cemetery.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You don't need to go into that, Mrs. Kolesar. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: BINAZIJA KOLESAR [Resumed]
utterances.text: On the 22nd of November, we arrived in Zagreb. I have been living in exile ever since.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you, Mrs. Kolesar. Just a few clarifying questions, please. You told me that you were on a -- on a bus that left the hospital compound together with your husband and others. How many buses were -- left the hospital compound for that purpose, about?

utterances.speaker: BINAZIJA KOLESAR [Resumed]
utterances.text: Five, I think.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Were they full --

utterances.speaker: BINAZIJA KOLESAR [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'm nearly certain there were five buses. Full. There weren't enough seats for everybody, but it was all right. We didn't mind.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And how many about people could it be in total on those buses?

utterances.speaker: BINAZIJA KOLESAR [Resumed]
utterances.text: If you bear in mind the fact that usually you can fit as many as 50 people on any one bus, then it would have been about 50 people. I really can't say at this moment. It was five times 50 people, five busloads of people totaling about 250 people, including doctors, nurses, our husbands, our children, newborn babies, nuns who were carrying those babies, pregnant women, and so on and so forth.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you, Mrs. Kolesar. You mentioned earlier about those buses. Did you see bus that were carrying you and the other as you just mentioned? When you were at the hospital compound or the hospital yard, did you see any other buses for any other purposes at the time?

utterances.speaker: BINAZIJA KOLESAR [Resumed]
utterances.text: Only those buses that we got onto left the hospital area and the bus that drove back to Serbia, the one bus that went back to Serbia. All the other vehicles that may have been outside in the courtyard, the military ambulances, I didn't see those. We encountered no military vehicles in the centre of town on our way to Negoslavci.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you, Mrs. Kolesar. Just also one -- the last clarification -- clarified question. You mentioned here people in white, the first time that you said you encountered the people in white. What was that? Can you explain the people in white, what that stands for?

utterances.speaker: BINAZIJA KOLESAR [Resumed]
utterances.text: When I say the people in white, I mean the so-called working group. We didn't know how the evacuation would unfold. They had been on standby as there were about 190 wounded who weren't able to walk. They were on standby to help transport the wounded. And even those who were able to walk but still needed to be assisted. They wore white coats and they were on standby for the transport or, rather, for the evacuation.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Okay. Mrs. Kolesar, thank you so much for this.

utterances.speaker: MS. TUMA
utterances.text: I have no further questions, thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. TUMA
utterances.text: And before that -- I'm sorry to interrupt, Your Honour. I would like to tender into evidence that chart that Mrs. Kolesar has been marking upon, and I would like to tender into evidence both the original one that has not been marked as well as the one that has been marked by Mrs. Kolesar.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: The --

utterances.speaker: MS. TUMA
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: -- sketch plan prepared by Ms. Kolesar and separately the marked sketch plan will be received in evidence.

utterances.speaker: MS. TUMA
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Those will be Exhibits number 48 and 49, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Thank you. Mrs. Kolesar, there will be, I expect, some further questions of you. First Mr. Vasic.

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honour. You're right. Cross-examined by Mr. Vasic:

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good afternoon, Mrs. Kolesar.

utterances.speaker: BINAZIJA KOLESAR [Resumed]
utterances.text: Good afternoon.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Let me first introduce myself. I'm attorney-at-law Miroslav Vasic, defending the accused Mrksic.

utterances.speaker: BINAZIJA KOLESAR [Resumed]
utterances.text: Good afternoon.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Before we start cross-examination, in view of the fact that both of us speak the same language, I would like to ask you to make a pause before answering my questions so that we can give a chance to interpreters to interpret what we say so that everybody else can follow.

utterances.speaker: BINAZIJA KOLESAR [Resumed]
utterances.text: I understood.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: First of all, I'd like to start from the end, from the point where you just concluded with my learned friend, when you arrived in Zagreb.

utterances.speaker: BINAZIJA KOLESAR [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You said that on the 22nd of November, you arrived in Zagreb where you reunited with your daughters, you and your husband.

utterances.speaker: BINAZIJA KOLESAR [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Can you tell me whether at some point in time upon your arrival in Zagreb you gave a statement to Croatian authorities relating to the events in Vukovar in October and November of 1991?

utterances.speaker: BINAZIJA KOLESAR [Resumed]
utterances.text: I must say I don't remember that.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did you perhaps, in June of 1992, so one year after your arrival in Zagreb, give a statement to Mr. Mladen Loncar?

utterances.speaker: BINAZIJA KOLESAR [Resumed]
utterances.text: Mladen Loncar came to the hospital where I worked, and he asked for my statement.
