utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: The statement focused on the events that you described today to this Trial Chamber?

utterances.speaker: BINAZIJA KOLESAR [Resumed]
utterances.text: Probably.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you. Do you remember giving a statement to the OTP investigators also about the events you described today?

utterances.speaker: BINAZIJA KOLESAR [Resumed]
utterances.text: All of us who left Vukovar were called to give a statement, but this didn't come about until 1995.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Yes, thank you. You are quite right. Another question concerning this. Do you know whether your husband gave a statement to The Hague Tribunal investigators?

utterances.speaker: BINAZIJA KOLESAR [Resumed]
utterances.text: Since I said that all of us who left Vukovar were asked to give a statement, that means that he was most likely asked to give it too. However, he's dead and I can no longer verify it with him.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you, Mrs. Kolesar. Now I would like to go back to something that preceded the events we discussed today. Would you agree with me that prior to these events Vukovar was a multi-ethnic city in which citizens of various ethnic backgrounds lived in harmony?

utterances.speaker: BINAZIJA KOLESAR [Resumed]
utterances.text: I could hold no other opinion.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I know that you were not involved in politics, but I suppose that just like all other citizens at the time you were informed about the political situation in your city.

utterances.speaker: BINAZIJA KOLESAR [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't think I can be considered to be not interested in what is going on around me, so, yes, I displayed some interest, was interested in what was accessible to me. I took in what I was interested in, change in the authorities, the various state changes and so on, but I took in only what I was interested in.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: In your opinion, was there a change in multi-ethnic relations after the first multi-party elections in which the HDZ party won, the Croatian Democratic Community party?

utterances.speaker: BINAZIJA KOLESAR [Resumed]
utterances.text: I must say that in Vukovar the SDP party won in the elections. I don't know whether you were aware of that. It wasn't the HDZ that won the elections in Vukovar.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Yes, madam. That was going to be another of my questions. I was interested in the elections at the republic level.

utterances.speaker: BINAZIJA KOLESAR [Resumed]
utterances.text: At the republic level, yes, the HDZ won. I think it also gained some seats in Vukovar, but as far as I know it was the SDP that won the elections -- in the elections.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You're quite right. I think that it was that party that won.

utterances.speaker: BINAZIJA KOLESAR [Resumed]
utterances.text: But nobody's status changed after the elections in Vukovar.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: After the victory of HDZ in the elections at the republic level was there any change in the constitution?

utterances.speaker: BINAZIJA KOLESAR [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think that is a normal result of election and normal consequence in the creation after new state.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Do you know whether those constitutional amendments also altered the status of the Serbian nation in the Republic of Croatia, which ceased to be a constituent nation, and that was the status it had according to the previous constitution?

utterances.speaker: MS. TUMA
utterances.text: Your Honour. Your Honour, I would like to object to this or ask a question of the relevance of those questions about the constitution. Mrs. Kolesar, she was a nurse at the hospital. Will she be able to give answers on the constitutional questions in this sense?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: I think two issues there, Mrs. Tuma, first whether Mrs. Kolesar is in a position to comment on that. The second is relevance. And you've mentioned both. Is there anything you wanted to say especially about relevance?

utterances.speaker: MS. TUMA
utterances.text: Yes, about the relevance, that -- I would say that Mrs. Kolesar, she is -- she was at the time working as a nurse at the hospital, and in that capacity can she give -- have any knowledge about the constitution of Croatia at the time?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Thank you, Mrs. Tuma. Please continue, Mr. Vasic, and we will learn quickly whether Mrs. Kolesar really knew anything about what was happening to the constitution. If she didn't, as Mrs. Tuma has pointed out, there's not much point in trying to ask her questions, but we will find out.

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I was about to say the following: I certainly didn't take the constitution into my hands and read it. Therefore, I didn't know what you're asking me about, whether there was an alteration you described. I simply wasn't interested in the constitution, not to that extent. I know that a new constitution was passed. That's all I know.

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you, madam.

utterances.speaker: BINAZIJA KOLESAR [Resumed]
utterances.text: You mentioned that in Vukovar the SDP party one in the elections, the party of democratic changes. Can you tell us who was elected president of Vukovar municipality?

utterances.speaker: BINAZIJA KOLESAR [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think that Slavko Dokmanovic was the president of municipality. And as for other offices, I really don't know who was a member of various committees and so on. I also don't know his term of office, and I can't go into this. My position and my job did not suffer any consequences from the changes that took place at the political level.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Yes, I understand what you're saying, madam. Thank you for your answer. At the time, you lived in Ivan Goran Kovacic Street; is that right?

utterances.speaker: BINAZIJA KOLESAR [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Do you know that at the time in your street members of Croatian ethnic group organised defence groups?

utterances.speaker: BINAZIJA KOLESAR [Resumed]
utterances.text: I really wouldn't know that. I didn't see anybody in my vicinity wearing any uniform. I didn't see any members of any organisations, and I passed through my street on a daily basis, yet I am not familiar with anything of the sort you're describing. I did not come across anybody who didn't live in that street.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Wasn't your husband a member of one such group, defence group, whose members didn't bear arms but were still members of the group established for that purpose?

utterances.speaker: BINAZIJA KOLESAR [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, sir.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did you ever speak to your husband about the statement he gave to the OTP investigators?

utterances.speaker: BINAZIJA KOLESAR [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. I didn't discuss my statement, and we simply did not discuss our statements.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You never discussed it.

utterances.speaker: BINAZIJA KOLESAR [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: But you know when he went to give a statement?

utterances.speaker: BINAZIJA KOLESAR [Resumed]
utterances.text: We went together.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Was your husband's first name Mihajlo?

utterances.speaker: BINAZIJA KOLESAR [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. May I ask something? My husband is dead. Can we not discuss him? Can he not be part of your questions? I would kindly ask that. He died four years ago, and please spare me the questions about him if at all possible.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Accept my sympathy, madam. I asked something that I thought you might know about, and then I had to proceed with my questions because you said you didn't know about that. I will not go into any of your painful memories unless absolutely necessary in this trial. Today, you told us that you were head nurse in the surgical ward of the Vukovar Medical Centre during the relevant period of time.

utterances.speaker: BINAZIJA KOLESAR [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You told us about the multi-ethnic composition of the hospital staff. Can you describe it further for us?

utterances.speaker: BINAZIJA KOLESAR [Resumed]
utterances.text: I couldn't give you the exact ratio, how many Serbs, how many Croats. I never was interested in statistics. All of us worked together, and these matters were not necessary in my view, at least within the scope of my work.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: After the event in Borovo Selo, did you perhaps notice that Serb doctors and nurses were leaving their jobs because they were afraid of the return of Ustashas who would slit their throats?

utterances.speaker: BINAZIJA KOLESAR [Resumed]
utterances.text: After the Borovo Selo incident, I have to tell you that I didn't go to Borovo Selo, Trpinja, or Brsadin. Based on the statements of people who were supposed to come to work, who were regular employees, it seems that they were unable to come to work because of the roadblocks in those villages. The propaganda spread around was such that it urged them to leave their jobs. I'm now relating to you what they told us. Therefore, those who didn't come to work had to have some kind of an excuse, because anybody who failed to show up for work for several days in a row could lose a job. So all of them came up with some excuses. Some of them came to work. Some did not come to work, claiming that they were prevented by roadblocks. I have to tell you that all the way up until the 20th of November we had at least 30 nurses in the hospital doing the same job with us, Serb nurses.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Madam, do you remember whether you said to the OTP investigators that after the killing of Croatian policemen in Borovo Selo on the 2nd of May, 1991, Serb doctors and nurses started leaving their jobs in the hospital citing that they were afraid of the return of Ustashas who would come back and slit their throats?

utterances.speaker: BINAZIJA KOLESAR [Resumed]
utterances.text: I am telling you that I conveyed the words of the persons who failed up -- who failed to show up for work and used these excuses. This is what they gave us as an excuse for not coming to work, when they called to give their excuses. Now, as to whether -- as to what they were told in their villages and what they heard is something I can't tell you anything about.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: But they gave you these excuses.

utterances.speaker: BINAZIJA KOLESAR [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. These are the excuses they gave. As to how they came with these excuses is something that you should ask them.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: At around May 1992 [as interpreted], did the Serb patients also stop coming to the Vukovar Medical Centre, or at least did their numbers decrease?

utterances.speaker: BINAZIJA KOLESAR [Resumed]
utterances.text: I have to answer by putting a question to you. If you yourself lived in Borovo Selo and if there was a roadblock there and if there was somebody at the roadblock preventing you from proceeding further, how would you go to the hospital?

utterances.speaker: MS. TUMA
utterances.text: Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Mrs. Tuma.

utterances.speaker: MS. TUMA
utterances.text: Yes. Thank you. Is says here on the transcript at around May 1992, and that is line 20. At around May 1992. Is it 1992 or -- is that the correct year? It's just a question.

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No, that's a mistake, but I can repeat my question. I think it has to do with 1991.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Thank you, Mrs. Tuma. And thank you, Mr. Vasic. I'd understood it as 1991, but maybe my mind was just anticipating yours.

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] It's been corrected. Thank you, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You believe that the only reason for the decrease in the numbers of Serb residents coming to the hospital were the roadblocks.

utterances.speaker: BINAZIJA KOLESAR [Resumed]
utterances.text: What else could it have been? We had doctors working in the hospital, Serbs, especially in the surgical ward. So what would the patients be afraid of in the hospital? You didn't ask me this, but I will tell you this. The surgical ward had to admit the wounded patients, and police had to secure the surgical ward. Other wards did not have any security personnel, but there is a rule, and I couldn't tell you anything more about this rule, that if we do admit wounded persons, then there must be police there to protect them, to guard them.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I assume these guards were armed.

utterances.speaker: BINAZIJA KOLESAR [Resumed]
utterances.text: I can't say whether there was someone walking around the surgery ward carrying a gun. I don't think that sort of armed presence was required. The fact that they were there was quite enough.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you for that answer. You mentioned roadblocks that prevented patients from coming to the hospital. Were the roadblocks being set up by both sides at the time, by Serbs wherever they happened to be the majority group and by Croats alike? What about the ones at Borovo Naselje?

utterances.speaker: BINAZIJA KOLESAR [Resumed]
utterances.text: I must say that I personally never saw a single roadblock, not in Borovo Naselje, not in Boro, not in Brsadin, not in Sotin or any other place because I didn't go anywhere. In July I had to Vinkovci. I went through Bogdanovci, Marinci, and Nustar, and there were no roadblocks along that particular road. I did not go to any other place, not even to Borovo Naselje. I didn't need to go there. It was that simple. I couldn't even describe a roadblock for you let alone how one is set up.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you. What about the health ministry of the republic in Croatia in the immediate aftermath of the 2nd of May events that we discussed? Did they in fact issue an order to establish a Crisis Staff at the Vukovar Medical Centre? You spoke about that, didn't you?

utterances.speaker: BINAZIJA KOLESAR [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that is true. That was probably just after. The surgery ward was not sufficiently prepared to take in all the wounded, and in my view it was necessary. I can't tell you if it was an order from the health ministry because I simply don't know, but I know that a Crisis Staff was established. Its task was to prepare the hospital for possible attacks and the need to move the wounded from the wards to the atomic shelter.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You will agree that at the time this decision was made and implemented there was still no armed clashes. The soldiers were still in the barracks. Tensions were running high between the ethnic groups but there was no armed conflict after the 2nd of May.

utterances.speaker: BINAZIJA KOLESAR [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'll disagree -- I'll disagree with you on one point. It's just simply not true that there were no soldiers around. I'm telling you this as an ordinary citizen who on my way back home from work regularly came across military vehicles, APCs, what have you. I was under the impression that those vehicles were heading for Borovo, Trpinja, or Brsadin, someplace in that general area. We came across a lot of those in town at the time, but like you stated, there were no particular clashes at this point.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: The preparations being carried out at the hospital, you said that these were only preparations for something that might happen, but didn't this escalate the conflict?

utterances.speaker: BINAZIJA KOLESAR [Resumed]
utterances.text: A hospital is certainly no place where a conflict might escalate. It becomes very important once the external conflict does escalate, but it certainly couldn't be called that. You must understand that a hospital must be ready for all eventualities. We didn't know what was in store for us, and once things started happening it would have been too late for us to do anything about it had we not started preparing in a timely fashion.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you, madam. You talked about members of the MUP who had been wounded and about their colleagues who provided safety at the hospital. What about the presence of these MUP members? Did that not cause disquiet among the Serbs in the hospital, especially after the 2nd of May?

utterances.speaker: BINAZIJA KOLESAR [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't think so. Those people, too, were citizens of Vukovar, and I think people of Serb ethnicity from Vukovar were familiar with these people. I don't think anybody was afraid of them, and it wasn't the way they acted while inside the hospital. They didn't act as if they had come there to protect us from something. They acted in a perfectly normal way, and there was no reason for them to act in any other way.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: At this point in time, changes occurred in the Ministry of the Interior of the Republic of Croatia, and very many Croats were recruited. Are you familiar with this fact?

utterances.speaker: BINAZIJA KOLESAR [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, you must believe that I know about everything if you're asking me this, but this is not something that I have ever heard.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Do you know anyone named Tomislav Mercep?

utterances.speaker: BINAZIJA KOLESAR [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. From the previous - what should I call it? - life, he was a person who worked for a firm called Borovski Gradjevina. It's a construction company. There were very few people who did not know him.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did he at one point become the secretary for the Defence Secretariat?

utterances.speaker: BINAZIJA KOLESAR [Resumed]
utterances.text: Probably so, but I didn't go there myself. There was no need for me to go there. I assume that might have been the case.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Was Mr. Mercep a generally known person in Vukovar?

utterances.speaker: BINAZIJA KOLESAR [Resumed]
utterances.text: I told you I knew this person from his civilian life. What happened to him later on, where he went later on, I have no idea. We -- our jobs had nothing in common, so I was in no position to keep tabs.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: During your stay in Vukovar in the autumn of 1991 and the summer of 1991, did you at any point, you or any member of your family, need to leave Vukovar?

utterances.speaker: BINAZIJA KOLESAR [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. I told you that I once went to Vinkovci in a private vehicle.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Are you familiar with the fact that --

utterances.speaker: BINAZIJA KOLESAR [Resumed]
utterances.text: But I didn't go anywhere else. I didn't go anywhere further afield. Even if authorisation was required to leave town, I had no reason to apply for one. I don't know if that was a requirement. If so, I don't know what it looked like or what it was used for.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did you in fact hear that someone did go and apply for authorisation and obtained one and from whom?

utterances.speaker: BINAZIJA KOLESAR [Resumed]
utterances.text: These were stories, rumours like the rumour about the Croatian soldiers coming into town to slit throats. I heard the same kind of story about these permits, passes. I can't answer this question because I don't know who prevented anyone else from leaving town. It's simply something that I'm not familiar with.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: What about May 1992? Did you listen to radio Vukovar --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: 1991, interpreter's correction.

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: -- at that point in time?

utterances.speaker: BINAZIJA KOLESAR [Resumed]
utterances.text: I did then and I still do.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did you know that on the 4th of May, 1991 its name was in fact changed?

utterances.speaker: BINAZIJA KOLESAR [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know. I can't say. I can't say that it wasn't, but I don't know that it was.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Do you know if the manager was changed or replaced?

utterances.speaker: BINAZIJA KOLESAR [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know that either.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You were asked by my learned friend in chief about Mr. Rade Popovic being replaced by Mrs. Vesna Bosanac who was appointed by the workers' council, and she became the chief of the Crisis Staff. Isn't that right?

utterances.speaker: BINAZIJA KOLESAR [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, but the same thing applied to Mr. Popovic before her, because the Crisis Staff was set up while he was still around.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And she continued these preparations that he had begun in May?

utterances.speaker: BINAZIJA KOLESAR [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, by all means.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did her husband do the same sort of thing, the same sort of preparations in Borovo Komerc? Is this something you're familiar with?

utterances.speaker: BINAZIJA KOLESAR [Resumed]
utterances.text: I have no idea. He was a civil engineer. He worked in the Borovo construction company but I know nothing about his specific duties.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: My apologies. I was pausing because I realised that the distinction between questions and answers was not entirely clear in the transcript. Did you know that in some parts of Vukovar, I'm talking about June and July 1991, explosive device were is planted in Serb-owned flats? Is it true that a Borba newsstand was mined? Is this something that you knew about?

utterances.speaker: BINAZIJA KOLESAR [Resumed]
utterances.text: Being a citizen of Vukovar, if nothing else I would have heard the explosions. Whose newsstand was it? Whose kiosks? Whose flats were those? If this is true I wasn't aware of that. If there's a powerful explosion of course you're likely to hear it. I don't believe the bit about flats, but if you say so, well -- I don't know. I really can't say.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You didn't hear stories, people talking about whose flats those were?

utterances.speaker: BINAZIJA KOLESAR [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: What about Borovo Naselje in July 1991? Did you hear anything about ethnic Serbs being cleansed from the area by members of the ZNG National Guards Corps?

utterances.speaker: BINAZIJA KOLESAR [Resumed]
utterances.text: First I hear of it.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you. Do you know that the army was stationed in the Vukovar barracks long before these events that we are discussing now?

utterances.speaker: BINAZIJA KOLESAR [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. The barracks was always there, but how many soldiers there were or what exactly the role of the barracks was is not something that I can talk about.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Do you know that in the summer of 1991 the ZNG, the National Guards Corps, laid siege to the barracks?

utterances.speaker: BINAZIJA KOLESAR [Resumed]
utterances.text: I know nothing about that. I'm not sure why I should be interested.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Well, the barracks is in the town of Vukovar. I thought that perhaps you would have learned something about it.

utterances.speaker: BINAZIJA KOLESAR [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, you're absolutely right. The barracks is in the town of Vukovar, but why would it matter to me whether it was blocked by someone or not? It made no difference whatsoever for me to be aware or know something like that.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did you ever hear about the National Guards Corps?

utterances.speaker: BINAZIJA KOLESAR [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. Of course I was aware of the National Guards Corps.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: This -- the National Guards Corps was established under the aegis of which political party? Do you know that?

utterances.speaker: BINAZIJA KOLESAR [Resumed]
utterances.text: I have no idea.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: What about its members? Which ethnic group did they belong to?

utterances.speaker: BINAZIJA KOLESAR [Resumed]
utterances.text: I knew of some National Guards Corps members who were actually Serbs. They were perhaps in the minority. And most of them were Croats, in case that's what you were asking.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Do you know about at one point in time in Vukovar the legally elected president of the Municipal Council was replaced by Croatia's government commissioner?

utterances.speaker: BINAZIJA KOLESAR [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I know that the government commissioner was appointed. I don't know when exactly, but I knew him personally because he was my children's schoolmate. That's how I learned about it. But I learned nothing about the way he was appointed or why.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Can you tell us which political party he belonged to?

utterances.speaker: BINAZIJA KOLESAR [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I can't say.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did you know that at one point the electricity and water supplies and phone lines were cut off in the barracks, after which the barracks was subjected to an attack by the National Guards Corps? This was something that happened in Vukovar, so I thought maybe you would know something about that.

utterances.speaker: BINAZIJA KOLESAR [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, it may have happened in Vukovar, but why would I be interested? I heard all sorts of stories that made no difference to me personally. Did this happen? When did it happen? It's not something that I can specify for you, or who the barracks was attacked by.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you, madam. I suppose you don't know whether these events, in fact, occurred before the JNA intervention in Vukovar.

utterances.speaker: BINAZIJA KOLESAR [Resumed]
utterances.text: I have no idea what you're talking about.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I'm talking about the attack on the barracks. Did this happen before the JNA stepped in or after? I suppose you don't know since you said you didn't know who had launched the attack.

utterances.speaker: BINAZIJA KOLESAR [Resumed]
utterances.text: You probably must think I'm pretty limited mentally, but I really have no idea what you're asking me. Which attack? The attack on the barracks?

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I'm asking you if the attack on the barracks was launched before the JNA attacked Vukovar.

utterances.speaker: BINAZIJA KOLESAR [Resumed]
utterances.text: I usually see the 25th of August as the starting date of the aggression against Vukovar. Are you referring to a period before that time? In that case, that is not something that I can talk about.

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, I'm not sure if this is a convenient time to break.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: That will do well, then, Mr. Vasic. We will resume at 5.45.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Mr. Vasic.

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I would like to go back to August 1991. From August until 18th of November, 1991, did you write down the names of the newly admitted wounded persons into the three notebooks that were kept as records in the hospital?

utterances.speaker: BINAZIJA KOLESAR [Resumed]
utterances.text: All of the wounded had to be registered in the official register book. From their personal details on to their diagnosis, everything else had to be registered. In addition to that, if they had a surgery that also needed to be noted down and any anaesthetic received, and if they had a plaster put on, that had to be registered as well. In order to make our job easier, we established these notebooks, so that if somebody came from another part of the town to inquire about whether a person was admitted, we had to have some lists, some notebooks that stayed close to us so that we wouldn't go and fetch the official register book every time. These were the so-called auxiliary books that we kept close to us so that we could answer any inquiries. So all of the information concerning the wounded persons were entered into several register books.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So you noted down all of this information into all books.

utterances.speaker: BINAZIJA KOLESAR [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that's right. From official register books down to all other notebooks.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Can you please tell us, what details were entered into these three notebooks?

utterances.speaker: BINAZIJA KOLESAR [Resumed]
utterances.text: Everything that was of importance for a particular person, anything that could be used in order to identify a person, to know more about a person. For example, name, residence, date of birth, place of birth, whether the person was civilian or was from police, for example, and so on. So if somebody came from police to inquire about a person, then we could provide all the information needed.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So you would also note down whether the person was a member of the ZNG or JNA?

utterances.speaker: BINAZIJA KOLESAR [Resumed]
utterances.text: Absolutely.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did you also register diagnosis or injuries?

utterances.speaker: BINAZIJA KOLESAR [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, why else would we need register books, because diagnosis is an essential part. Without diagnosis there can be no injuries.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Yes. I absolutely agree with you. It's just that you omitted to mention that in your answer.

utterances.speaker: BINAZIJA KOLESAR [Resumed]
utterances.text: I apologise.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So if you had these books on you, then you were able to provide all information about a certain patient, whether he was a member of the ZNG, JNA police force, name, other details and so on.

utterances.speaker: BINAZIJA KOLESAR [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. I expect that somebody would be kind enough to return these notebooks back to us because it is extremely important for us to know more about injuries, and our doctors would be able to use these notebooks for their further work so that the picture of everything that was going on would be finally full and clear.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You said that on the 17th of November the combat operations ceased. Can we agree that no further patients were admitted into hospital after this day?

utterances.speaker: BINAZIJA KOLESAR [Resumed]
utterances.text: There were no newly wounded persons. However, persons who needed to have their wounds re-bandaged came to the hospital for treatment.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: In the beginning of cross-examination I asked you about the statement you gave in Zagreb to Mr. Mladen Loncar. In that statement, did you say that on the day of evacuation there was a total of 100 -- 290 patients and wounded, 190 of whom were those in beds and 100 were those who were able to move?

utterances.speaker: BINAZIJA KOLESAR [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'm unable to recall that fact. I can't confirm it. This is something that I stated based on my then recollection. But the fact is that we believe that on the day of the fall of Vukovar there was about 400 wounded in the hospital.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Yesterday, you said that in the 400 you counted also newborn babies and so on?

utterances.speaker: BINAZIJA KOLESAR [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that's right. So this number reflects the wounded and the ill.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So that's why I'm asking you whether it is possible that there were 290 wounded. This is the figure that you gave in Zagreb.

utterances.speaker: BINAZIJA KOLESAR [Resumed]
utterances.text: There were about 400 of them in total. I know that we had 14 newborns. I don't know how many pregnant women. We also had persons in the internal diseases ward and so on. So we had to put this down on paper and say this many wounded and this many other patients.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So do you remember this statement that you gave in Zagreb? Do you remember stating this?

utterances.speaker: BINAZIJA KOLESAR [Resumed]
utterances.text: I can't remember the figure I gave. How can you expect one to remember that after 14 years? I probably did have a figure that we used in our assessments, but I wouldn't be able to confirm the figure you gave me just now.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Do you remember discussing this in Zagreb with Mr. Loncar, the total figure?

utterances.speaker: BINAZIJA KOLESAR [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'm sure we discussed all events in Vukovar. I wasn't the only person who was able to give the figure. There were many of us who knew the figure. Now that 14 years have passed, it is difficult to say this is exactly how things transpired. Those who are able to say that are quite unique.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Would you want me to show you your statement?

utterances.speaker: BINAZIJA KOLESAR [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, no need. What would I do with it? I'm not claiming that I didn't state that. I'm not claiming that. Now, as to how accurate that figure is, it's hard to say.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you. I'd like to ask you now something relating to the patients in the hospital and the evacuations. You said that in October of 1991, a convoy was organised by Medicins Sans Frontieres who took away 112 patients.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: All right. 112 patients were evacuated from Vukovar Hospital. Is the name of Ivan Zivkovic familiar to you? He was a soldier treated in your hospital.

utterances.speaker: BINAZIJA KOLESAR [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. It doesn't sound familiar.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Do you know whether he was included in the convoy that left Vukovar and went to Vinkovci?

utterances.speaker: BINAZIJA KOLESAR [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't remember the name from the list. And why do I claim that there were 112? I received this information subsequently from the then officer of the JNA who was a liaison officer escorting the convoy. Perhaps sometime in 1995 or 1996 he brought the list of names to me, the list that he compiled personally. He was an officer of the JNA. This is why I know the exact figure. Had I known you were interested in the names, I could have brought the list with me.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You mentioned the list. Do you have it with you in The Hague?

utterances.speaker: BINAZIJA KOLESAR [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. What would I do with it here?

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Can you tell us who was the officer who gave you the list? Was he from the medical corps?

utterances.speaker: BINAZIJA KOLESAR [Resumed]
utterances.text: I wouldn't know. For a long time I didn't even know his name, but he called me on the phone, gave me his name. He has left the JNA in the meantime. He has a master's degree in economics, runs a private firm, and I don't know his name just now off-the-cuff.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: If you know his name, we can go into private session.

utterances.speaker: BINAZIJA KOLESAR [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know the name. I don't know it by heart. It's quite hard to remember all of these things. Why would I try to remember them if I can write them down?

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Where do you have all this information? In your house?

utterances.speaker: BINAZIJA KOLESAR [Resumed]
utterances.text: Why are you interested in this?

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I would like to know when you would be able to deliver this to us.

utterances.speaker: BINAZIJA KOLESAR [Resumed]
utterances.text: If you conclude your cross-examination tonight and I go home tomorrow, I would be able to provide it to you the day after tomorrow.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you. Let us go back to this soldier, Ivan Zivkovic. He was wounded and was treated in the hospital, guarded by the ZNG. Are you aware of this? Do you remember this?

utterances.speaker: BINAZIJA KOLESAR [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. There was not a single wounded person of any ethnic background who was guarded by anybody. No, we had no such cases.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Do you know the name of soldier Sasa Jovic who was a patient in your hospital?

utterances.speaker: BINAZIJA KOLESAR [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Was he there together with other two members of the JNA in your hospital?

utterances.speaker: BINAZIJA KOLESAR [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Up until the 19th of November, were they guarded by Damir Samardzic known as Veliki Bojler, ZNG member?

utterances.speaker: BINAZIJA KOLESAR [Resumed]
utterances.text: That is possible, but I am not aware of that. I know the nurse who took care of them. As for who guarded them, I wouldn't know. I don't think there was any need for anyone to guard them. And if somebody was assigned to do that, that was none of my business. I took care of nursing service.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Can you tell us who was the nurse who took care of them?

utterances.speaker: BINAZIJA KOLESAR [Resumed]
utterances.text: Nurse Ilonka Novak [phoen].

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did you ever see any ZNG members guarding any wounded persons?

utterances.speaker: BINAZIJA KOLESAR [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. No soldiers were there alone, so they couldn't guard just one person. They had to guard everybody else who was there. So if there was a person there, then that person was guarding everybody who was in there.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: These three soldiers, Jovic, Sasa, and the other two, were they kept separately? Were they placed in a separate room guarded by Dvor Samardzic?

utterances.speaker: BINAZIJA KOLESAR [Resumed]
utterances.text: They did indeed have their own room. They were quite lucky to have it. We were able to provide a room to them. Not because somebody had to guard them but that -- so that they could have their peace, that they could have a calm environment and that they could have a nurse taking care of them. They were not placed in that room in order to isolate them. What I can tell you is that room in which they were was shelled and destroyed. Fortunately, they had been taken out of their room. And then their room was shelled another time. Another shell landed in their room, and fortunately they were not there. The remaining time they spent together with all other patients until the 18th of November. They smoked the same cigarettes as everybody else did and had a much less comfortable situation afterwards.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Was some kind of Serbian lobby accused for everything that was happening there?

utterances.speaker: BINAZIJA KOLESAR [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, nobody was accused. But if a shell landed several times in the same place, then naturally people started wondering whether somebody was providing information.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Who constituted this Serbian lobby? Who represented the Serbian lobby in the hospital?

utterances.speaker: BINAZIJA KOLESAR [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't think there was Serbian lobby. We just had Serbian or Serb staff members.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So these suspicions that you had were erroneous.

utterances.speaker: BINAZIJA KOLESAR [Resumed]
utterances.text: I can't say that there were any suspicions. Nothing of that nature was organised. It could have been a Croat who reported this. So, yes, I can have my suspicions, but I can't prove them.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Is the name of soldier Slavomir Bestin [phoen] and Milan Biber familiar to you, these two names? Those were the people who were admitted on the 25th of August?

utterances.speaker: BINAZIJA KOLESAR [Resumed]
utterances.text: I can't claim that such people weren't admitted, but you can hardly expect me to remember all of the people. I can't say that they were not among the wounded.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Can you tell us how many JNA members were wounded and admitted in the Vukovar Hospital?

utterances.speaker: BINAZIJA KOLESAR [Resumed]
utterances.text: I wouldn't be able to give you the exact figure. I can remember only those who stayed longer in the hospital; for example, the three you mentioned. We had more contacts with them. Those who spent only one day, we don't remember. I didn't have special records pertaining to the JNA. I don't think that anybody else kept such special records.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Those soldiers who spent only one day in the hospital, what happened to them afterwards?

utterances.speaker: BINAZIJA KOLESAR [Resumed]
utterances.text: I suppose that you're asking me about these who were wounded on the 25th. The wounded who were admitted at the time were perhaps evacuated, or perhaps the army came to fetch them, or they were taken to the hospital in Vinkovci if their injuries justified that.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Were they perhaps taken to Zagreb?

utterances.speaker: BINAZIJA KOLESAR [Resumed]
utterances.text: Probably not that far. They were most likely taken to the nearest hospital so that the other hospital would then decide what to do with them.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I'm waiting for the interpretation to finish before continuing.

utterances.speaker: BINAZIJA KOLESAR [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I'm aware of that.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: The name of soldier Nedeljko Turekalo [phoen], is it familiar to you?

utterances.speaker: BINAZIJA KOLESAR [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: All right. You don't remember this soldier. Let me ask you then those that you do remember, Jovic, Sasa, and the other two.

utterances.speaker: BINAZIJA KOLESAR [Resumed]
utterances.text: May I put a question? How can anyone expect someone to remember the names so well? I can remember the name of a person whom I knew before. Yes, I would remember such a name. But somebody who I meet for the first time, it is very difficult to remember that name for a long period of time regardless of who the person belonged to, the JNA, the National Guards Corps, and so on.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I'm just trying to determine what you know. I'm not asking you to remember something you can't remember. So let us go back to the ones you remember, soldier Sasa Jovic. Do you remember whether he was exclusively treated by Dr. Njavro?

utterances.speaker: BINAZIJA KOLESAR [Resumed]
utterances.text: Not just he but all three of them, because they were in the same room.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Who assigned Dr. Njavro to treat the three of them?

utterances.speaker: BINAZIJA KOLESAR [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know. And is there anything bad about him treating them? That's my question.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I didn't say there was anything bad about it. I'm just putting a question to you. Do you know the name of Branko Stankovic?

utterances.speaker: BINAZIJA KOLESAR [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Tomo Jakoljevic [phoen], a patient of your hospital?

utterances.speaker: BINAZIJA KOLESAR [Resumed]
utterances.text: I know Tomo Jakoljevic from before. He was our plaster technician. We used to work for years together.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Do you know what happened to him later?

utterances.speaker: BINAZIJA KOLESAR [Resumed]
utterances.text: He was wounded in his leg. I think that a leg was amputated around his ankle. After the treatment was concluded, he was transferred to our I will call it auxiliary hospital, which was a hospital for the wounded who no longer required intensive care. This hospital was located in Borovo Komerc.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Is he still alive?

utterances.speaker: BINAZIJA KOLESAR [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know that.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Can you tell me who was in charge of that hospital in Borovo Komerc?

utterances.speaker: BINAZIJA KOLESAR [Resumed]
utterances.text: Our doctors were there. Who was in charge and took care of the food and so on, I wouldn't know that, but we had our team of doctors there, an orthopaedist and several other specialists. Not surgeons but other specialists and nurses. They were able to bandage patients there, provide therapy, and so on.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You said that after the 17th of November there were no more new patients arriving in the hospital. What about civilians and members of the MUP and ZNG? Did they start arriving in great numbers?

utterances.speaker: BINAZIJA KOLESAR [Resumed]
utterances.text: Civilians in great numbers, yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: What about the ZNG and the MUP?

utterances.speaker: BINAZIJA KOLESAR [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know about the ZNG, and the MUP people arrived because their building had burned down. It had been shelled and destroyed. It burnt to the ground. They had to come to the hospital. Some of them were wounded.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: When did these people from the MUP come to the hospital?

utterances.speaker: BINAZIJA KOLESAR [Resumed]
utterances.text: I can't be specific about the date, whether it was the 17th, the 16th, or the 18th. I really don't know. I don't even know how many of them arrived.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You did not see a single ZNG member arrive in the hospital in uniform?

utterances.speaker: BINAZIJA KOLESAR [Resumed]
utterances.text: You mean coming just like that saying, "Here I am," no. I didn't see a single one. I don't know what such a person would be doing wearing a uniform in the hospital to begin with.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: For example, if this person wanted to change his clothes. Do you know that some of the ZNG members changed their clothes in the hospital?

utterances.speaker: BINAZIJA KOLESAR [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know about the ZNG members doing that. I know about some of the guards.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: What did they put on?

utterances.speaker: BINAZIJA KOLESAR [Resumed]
utterances.text: Their civilian clothes. Some clothes. I don't know where they got them. Some put on their track suits, whatever was handy.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did some of these persons who arrived after the 17th of November put on white coats?

utterances.speaker: BINAZIJA KOLESAR [Resumed]
utterances.text: I find that difficult to believe. I can't say. White coats were usually worn by people who were in charge of transporting the wounded. I really can't say whether any one of those who arrived put on a white coat. There were a lot of people there, too many for me to say whether any of them at any given point in time put on a white coat.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Were they in a position to be involved in the transport of the wounded?

utterances.speaker: BINAZIJA KOLESAR [Resumed]
utterances.text: If they'd been assigned by someone.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So it's possible that they had been assign by someone to do that. They were physically able to help with the transport of the wounded.

utterances.speaker: BINAZIJA KOLESAR [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, but if so, I was certainly not aware of that.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did you ever believe that some of the people who put on these white coats were later killed because of that, that it cost them their lives? Did you ever state anything like this to anyone?

utterances.speaker: BINAZIJA KOLESAR [Resumed]
utterances.text: I can't remember. I don't know whether I could have said something like that but it's possible.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: What could have led you to believe something like that?

utterances.speaker: BINAZIJA KOLESAR [Resumed]
utterances.text: Can I tell you? I read something to the effect. I read an article written by Dr. Ivankovic in which he states in no uncertain terms when the medical staff entered the plaster room it was only then that you could see who was who. That's his statement, so I'm using it to conclude that this may, after all, have cost someone their life. Prior to finding out about this statement, it would never had occurred to me.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I apologise. Did you know that any of these newly arrived persons pretended that they were wounded by putting bandages on?

utterances.speaker: BINAZIJA KOLESAR [Resumed]
utterances.text: There is no way anyone can pretend to be wounded like that. You can only be classified as wounded if someone looks at you and writes up a diagnosis. You can't put on a plaster cast just like that or conduct a medical examination. There must be a document to the effect showing that you were in fact wounded. But if you were in the hospital, it means you had a document to show that you were wounded.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Do you know the name Josip Bradaric?

utterances.speaker: BINAZIJA KOLESAR [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You refer to him in your statement?

utterances.speaker: BINAZIJA KOLESAR [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Was he a member of the MUP?

utterances.speaker: BINAZIJA KOLESAR [Resumed]
utterances.text: I really can't say. I think he was in the police before the war, but I can't be certain about it.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Do you know that the medical workers cut him up and stitched his wounds so as to make it look as if he'd been wounded?

utterances.speaker: BINAZIJA KOLESAR [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know. My personal impression was that one of the tasks that Dr. Ivezic had was to check whether people were really wounded or not. I was very pleased that the first person he looked at did have an obvious wound, an injury to the eye, plus a statement by the doctor who dressed his arm. All I can say about this is what I saw with my own eyes. If somebody actually self-inflicted a wound, then only they would know, but I'm certainly in no position to ascertain that.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: When you spoke to the OTP investigator in June 1995, did you tell them that you were afraid what would happen if somebody found out that Josip was not really wounded?

utterances.speaker: BINAZIJA KOLESAR [Resumed]
utterances.text: Of course I was afraid. Imagine there's an inspection, and he doesn't have a bandage, has nothing on at all, but I was very pleased to see that he did have all of these things.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: How did it occur to you to begin with that he may not have been wounded if he was registered as wounded?

utterances.speaker: BINAZIJA KOLESAR [Resumed]
utterances.text: It's not Mr. Bradaric I'm talking about. I'm talking about the rumour. This again is a rumour. Somebody wants to pretend they are wounded. So I'm playing along these lines. But if the wound is there, if the diagnosis is there, then I'm very pleased.

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Can we please go into private session briefly.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Private.

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Do you know if Dr. Tomic compiled any lists?

utterances.speaker: BINAZIJA KOLESAR [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. He was one of the doctors who did. He is available. You can call him and ask him what he did.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did you know that Miroslav Kosir took off his MUP uniform, put on his civilian clothes and left the hospital on the 19th?

utterances.speaker: BINAZIJA KOLESAR [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, indeed. Miroslav Kosir is still a neighbour of mine. If I may be allowed to add, he got a change of clothes. He was a guard at the hospital carrying no weapons. He was unarmed. His family entered the hospital with the group of civilians. He changed into civilian clothes, and he left the hospital with them. He ended up in a Serb camp. He didn't go straight home but at least he survived.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Are you talking about the evacuation that was conducted by Zeljka -- and organised by Zeljka Zgonjanin?

utterances.speaker: BINAZIJA KOLESAR [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that's the one.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: When asked by the OTP investigators about the wounded, did you not state that at the hospital it was difficult to say at the time who was really wounded and who was just pretending?

utterances.speaker: BINAZIJA KOLESAR [Resumed]
utterances.text: I may have said it, but I don't remember whether I did or not. It's very difficult to remember exactly what I said at the time and if it has been taken out of context. What can be said is that each wounded appearing on the list that we have discussed need have been diagnosed as wounded. No doctor could have placed them on one of the lists if they were not really wounded. And then a doctor would make the usual rounds and establish whether all of them were authentically wounded. The rest of us were only in a position to hear rumours, if that.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did Colonel Ivezic come with that list in order to express his suspicion that some of these persons on the list were in fact not wounded?

utterances.speaker: BINAZIJA KOLESAR [Resumed]
utterances.text: I would just love to know what exactly his remit was, whether to verify the authenticity of the list and if the people were wounded or not. If so, the ones that he looked at and saw for himself that they were indeed wounded, I would love to know what happened to those people and what sort of a doctor he was.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Does the name Josip Covic, a ZNG member, ring a bell?

utterances.speaker: BINAZIJA KOLESAR [Resumed]
utterances.text: Josip Covic. I really can't say. I don't know.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: What about the name Vilem Karlovic [phoen]?

utterances.speaker: BINAZIJA KOLESAR [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Just to wrap it up, you're not claiming that members of the ZNG and MUP did not in fact change their clothes in the hospital. You're just saying you don't know whether there was or there wasn't.

utterances.speaker: BINAZIJA KOLESAR [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'm not aware that any ZNG members changed their clothes, but I happened to work in the vicinity of people who were wearing police uniforms, who were unarmed, who were, for example, guarding Dr. Vesna Bosanac's door and the entrance of the emergency ward. They were unarmed, and yes, of course, I did see them in civilian clothes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: What about the names Emil Cakalic, Mladen Muklarik [phoen]? Do these ring a bell? Were they patients of the hospital?

utterances.speaker: BINAZIJA KOLESAR [Resumed]
utterances.text: I know Emil Cakalic from before. He used to have a lab technician with us, and later he was a health inspector. I never saw him among the wounded or among the patients. He may have been in the hospital at the time, but that does not necessarily imply that we ran into each other.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Was he on the list of wounded people that you had tied up?

utterances.speaker: BINAZIJA KOLESAR [Resumed]
utterances.text: I can't remember that. I would need to go back to the list in order to verify that.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: There's one thing that's not in the transcript. I was talking about Emil Cakalic.

utterances.speaker: BINAZIJA KOLESAR [Resumed]
utterances.text: Regardless of the fact that he was a health inspector. If he was wounded, then there had to be some sort of a medical history or a diagnosis. He couldn't just walk in there saying I'm wounded.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I'm not saying this. I'm just asking whether you know this or not.

utterances.speaker: BINAZIJA KOLESAR [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Was each doctor individually responsible for any evacuation lists they compiled?

utterances.speaker: BINAZIJA KOLESAR [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I believe so.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And the lists were not compared or coordinated for greater accuracy?

utterances.speaker: BINAZIJA KOLESAR [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. How could they have been compared? Each doctor had his own group of wounded to go through, and this was their own personal responsibility. The only thing that could have been the case is for a different group of doctors to go and run the same check.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You mentioned that the evacuation was schedule for the 19th of November, 1991, and was postponed for one day. Do you know whether the evacuation was in fact postponed to give the military a time to clear the mines near the town walls?

utterances.speaker: BINAZIJA KOLESAR [Resumed]
utterances.text: I have no idea where these town walls are supposed to be. If you tell me that, perhaps I could answer your question.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Between Marinci and Sinovci.

utterances.speaker: BINAZIJA KOLESAR [Resumed]
utterances.text: I really don't know.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: On the road to Vinkovci.

utterances.speaker: BINAZIJA KOLESAR [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, that may well be the case. I go to Vinkovci every day but I'm not familiar with this location. Once I'm back, I'll try to find out.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did you know that a convoy that left for Vinkovci in the afternoon was returned and eventually drove to Sremska Mitrovica because they came under fire by the Croatian side, which was coordinated by the ECMM?

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Could the speakers please speak one at a time to ensure accurate interpretation.

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: From the town of Vukovar itself, yes.

utterances.speaker: BINAZIJA KOLESAR [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know that a convoy ever left. I only heard some stories that there were some JNA medical vehicles. They left for Bogdanovci and then drove back to the hospital. That was the story I heard, but I know nothing else. I'm not familiar with any details. I wasn't part of this convoy, and I can't tell you anything. Rumour has it that the wounded were there, that our employees were there, that they went there and turned back and then drove on to Mitrovica, but those who were actually a part of the convoy should be able to provide more detail.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Do you know who was part of convoy?

utterances.speaker: BINAZIJA KOLESAR [Resumed]
utterances.text: One person I know is Stefan Biro. I don't know about the others.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you. Do you know that in the afternoon of the 19th of November food and water arrived in the hospital?

utterances.speaker: BINAZIJA KOLESAR [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. I didn't see that. I didn't hear that anybody went to fetch the food and water.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Do you know that before the 18th of November the entire command structure of Vukovar defence left the city?

utterances.speaker: BINAZIJA KOLESAR [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I know that.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Do you know that Mr. Borkovic, known as Mladi Jastreb [phoen] cut the telephone lines of the hospital and that he did the same thing in relation to the MUP building?

utterances.speaker: BINAZIJA KOLESAR [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I don't know about that.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You told us about the three notebooks, about register books. In addition to those, were any other records kept?

utterances.speaker: BINAZIJA KOLESAR [Resumed]
utterances.text: We had the records of the deceased in the hospital, which was done by the police inspector Tomislav Hegedus. While we were able to bury the deceased or those who were killed, they were buried either in the old hospital graveyard or on the stadium. While this was conducted, he kept the records of those who had been buried.

utterances.speaker: MS. TUMA
utterances.text: Your Honour. I'm sorry, I have to interrupt here.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Yes, Mrs. Tuma.

utterances.speaker: MS. TUMA
utterances.text: The witness here named one witness here. Just a moment, please.

utterances.speaker: MS. TUMA
utterances.text: I'm sorry. I withdraw that. I'm sorry. So please continue.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: I take it you were concerned there might have been naming of a protected witness. Sorry for that it seems, Mr. Vasic. Carry on.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No, no. The person I mentioned has not yet been located or identified. We don't know whether this person was killed. Therefore, the inspector was tasked with keeping the record of those who had been buried. So if I knew about somebody who was buried, I had to remember the number so that later on when normal conditions were reinstated we would be able to stay person buried under such-and-such name was such-and-such -- under such-and-such number was of that identity. However, due to numerous attacks in the area, we were unable to continue with the burials. We ran out of space. So a location closer to us was picked which was the port authority near the Danube River. We started burying the deceased and those who were killed there. However, two or three persons were killed as they were burying people, and we had to stop with that activity. So the deceased or those who were killed were simply placed in the entrance of the port authority building which was across the road from the hospital. Unfortunately, in those last few days before the fall of Vukovar, we were unable to do anything else. The other type of record was kept by another inspector who again for the purposes of police kept record of those who were wounded. So that, for example, if a wounded member of ZNG or police force was admitted, then inspector would take over that person's weapon and belongings. All of that would be duly recorded, and thus us civilians didn't have to deal with that. He as police inspector took care of that. Inspector -- this inspector is no longer alive either. I don't know whether he has been identified.

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: The documentation that you mentioned, did you bring it with you or did that remain in the hospital?

utterances.speaker: BINAZIJA KOLESAR [Resumed]
utterances.text: Everything remain in the hospital.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you. Could you tell us whether Mrs. Vesna Bosanac, in addition to being director of the hospital and chief of the Crisis Staff, was she also a member of the Crisis Staff of the Vukovar defence?

utterances.speaker: BINAZIJA KOLESAR [Resumed]
utterances.text: I wouldn't be able to tell you that. I don't know. I think that Dr. Ivica Matos was a member. I know this from him. I heard it from him, because he would convey various orders to us. "We have to prepare the shelter. Is the hospital ready," and so on. He conveyed this to us as member of the Municipal Staff. As for Dr. Bosanac, he was -- she was the chief of the Crisis Staff ex officio, not because she was appointed to that position.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did she inform the staff about the content of the appeals sent by her?

utterances.speaker: BINAZIJA KOLESAR [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know about that.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: These appeals, weren't they sent out on behalf of the hospital Crisis Staff?

utterances.speaker: BINAZIJA KOLESAR [Resumed]
utterances.text: They were signed by Dr. Bosanac.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did Dr. Jure Njavro have exclusive right to perform surgeries on the wounded ZNG members? Do you know anything about that?

utterances.speaker: BINAZIJA KOLESAR [Resumed]
utterances.text: Exclusive right? No, I don't think that such a thing existed. He was appointed chief surgeon. Have for the exclusive right to operate, no. Everybody performed surgeries. He was perhaps the one who set up teams and allocated work. And as for him being the only person authorised to operate on people, no.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Who appointed him chief war surgeon?

utterances.speaker: BINAZIJA KOLESAR [Resumed]
utterances.text: The director did.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did she consult somebody before doing that?

utterances.speaker: BINAZIJA KOLESAR [Resumed]
utterances.text: I wouldn't be able to say.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Cuckovic, does that last name mean anything to you? He was a wounded -- or he was a worker in the hospital.

utterances.speaker: BINAZIJA KOLESAR [Resumed]
utterances.text: We had several workers with that last name. Throughout the occupation, we had a plaster technician, Djuro Cuckovic, and his son was a driver in the hospital. The son's name was Dusko. On the 19th of November, the nurses who were on the ground floor of the hospital facing the courtyard called me because they had recognised Dusan Cuckovic. He wore a camouflage uniform and was digging through the trash. We didn't know why he did that. I didn't see him enter the hospital building even though his father worked in the surgical clinic.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Do you know that ZNG uniforms were found on the -- on the refuse site?

utterances.speaker: BINAZIJA KOLESAR [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I don't know about that but that is possible. We had to discard things somewhere. It is improper to keep unsanitary things in the hospital. And I personally didn't go through the trash so I wouldn't be able to tell you what exactly was there.

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, could we go into private session once again, please. I have two more questions --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Private.

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] -- for the witness.

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Finally, I would like to put questions to the witness relating to the statement she gave to the OTP investigators. Could the usher please distribute hard copies to all the parties. This document is marked in the electronic database. The English version is 2D010048, and B/C/S version is 2D010036. Could we be shown these documents on the screen, please.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Mrs. Kolesar, do you have a copy before you?

utterances.speaker: BINAZIJA KOLESAR [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Could you please take a look at the English version of this statement and verify whether your signature is at the bottom of each page.

utterances.speaker: BINAZIJA KOLESAR [Resumed]
utterances.text: I have Croatian version before me and there are no signatures on it.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: That's because the English version is the original. Just a minute, please. Madam, can you please take a look at the screen.

utterances.speaker: BINAZIJA KOLESAR [Resumed]
utterances.text: There's nothing on the screen.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: We have to wait a bit.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: I understand, Mr. Vasic, that both the English and the B/C/S version are with the witness, but coming up now on the screen is the English. There was a delay while the witness's screen was being connected technically.

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, I have to ask the witness whether she can see the English version on her screen.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I can see the English version, and if BK stands for my signature, it could be. It doesn't have to be. We would need a graphologist to examine this. And as to why there are only initials BK here, it's hard to say.

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Could we be shown 2D010056 on the screen. This is the last page of this document and it reflects your full signature. Can you see it, Mrs. Kolesar?

utterances.speaker: BINAZIJA KOLESAR [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. This up here is my signature.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you. Is this the statement you gave to The Hague investigators on the 19th and 20th of June, 1995?

utterances.speaker: BINAZIJA KOLESAR [Resumed]
utterances.text: Most likely it is.

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, I don't have any further questions for the witness. I would like to tender this statement into evidence.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: On what basis do you wish to tender the statement, Mr. Vasic?

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] In my cross-examination I asked the witness many things about topics covered in the statement, and she provided answers that differ from the ones in the statement. On those occasions, I told her I was quoting from her statement.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Mr. Vasic, I'm afraid you won't be able to sit down or you may not be able to at this moment. The appropriate procedure for you now under the jurisprudence of this Tribunal is for you -- if the witness has given an account that you believe to be different from what she said in the statement to show her the passage in the statement and then ask for her comment on the difference, and do that for each important difference that you wish to bring to the Chamber's attention. And normally, as the Appeals Chamber has indicated, by that means the record of your cross-examination will reveal each of the material differences you have identified between the present evidence and the earlier statement, and by that means all parties and the Chamber have a full record of any differences when we come to the end of the trial and have to look at the ultimate questions. And as the Appeals Chamber has indicated, normally the statement itself is not properly admitted into evidence. So it's important that you identify item by item the material differences and have that recorded. So I'm sorry. It's -- if you want to do that, it will mean going through the particular passages in the statement. And I hope that all counsel will note that, so that if they need to do that with this or any other statement or other document that they will appreciate the proper procedure to follow. Are you ready to do that if you wish to now, Mr. Vasic, or would you prefer to do that in the morning? Sorry, tomorrow afternoon. I just don't know whether you're prepared to do that now, and I wouldn't want to --

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, we could do it tomorrow afternoon then.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Very well.

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Given the time that we have now.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: I think that will help you be more specifically prepared for it and should save time in the long-run. We must, then, adjourn now a few minutes early but hopefully with the object of saving time ultimately. Mrs. Kolesar, I'm afraid I must ask you to return tomorrow afternoon to continue your evidence. We will be commencing again at 2.15.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
